arXiv:2407.10356v2 [math-ph] 12 Sep 2025

Surprising symmetry properties and exact solutions
of Kolmogorov backward equations
with power diffusivity

Serhii D. Koval†‡, Elsa Dos Santos Cardoso-Bihlo† and Roman O. Popovych§‡

†Department of Mathematics and Statistics, Memorial University of Newfoundland,
  St. John’s (NL) A1C 5S7, Canada

§ Mathematical Institute, Silesian University in Opava, Na Rybníčku 1, 746 01 Opava, Czech Republic

‡ Institute of Mathematics of NAS of Ukraine, 3 Tereshchenkivska Str., 01024 Kyiv, Ukraine

E-mails: skoval@mun.ca, ecardosobihl@mun.ca, rop@imath.kiev.ua

Using the original advanced version of the direct method, we efficiently compute the equivalence groupoids and equivalence groups of two peculiar classes of Kolmogorov backward equations with power diffusivity and solve the problems of their complete group classifications. The results on the equivalence groups are double-checked with the algebraic method. Within these classes, the remarkable Fokker–Planck and the fine Kolmogorov backward equations are distinguished by their exceptional symmetry properties. We extend the known results on these two equations to their counterparts with respect to a nontrivial discrete equivalence transformation. Additionally, we carry out Lie reductions of the equations under consideration up to the point equivalence, exhaustively study their hidden Lie symmetries and generate wider families of their new exact solutions via acting by their recursion operators on constructed Lie-invariant solutions. This analysis reveals eight powers of the space variable with exponents −1-1, 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6 as values of the diffusion coefficient that are prominent due to symmetry properties of the corresponding equations.

1 Introduction

The Kolmogorov backward equations originated from the foundational work by Kolmogorov [26], where he extended the theory of discrete-time Markov processes to its continuous counterpart. Among the latter, Kolmogorov distinguished diffusion processes and, for describing their evolution, derived a pair of classes of equations, usually referred to as Kolmogorov forward (or Fokker–Planck) and Kolmogorov backward equations. Since these equations capture fundamental features of diffusion processes, they became the cornerstones of many branches of physics, natural sciences and even economics. For instance, in physics these equations are instrumental in modeling lasers and other nonlinear systems far from thermal equilibrium [49, Chapter 12]. Specifically for the Kolmogorov backward equations, they are applied in evolutionary biology, ecology and environmental science to model and predict the dynamics of ecosystems and populations.

In the present paper, we carry out extended symmetry analysis of the ultraparabolic (1+2)-dimensional Kolmogorov backward equations of the form

ℱα​β:ut+x​uy=|x−α|β​ux​x,\displaystyle\mathcal{F}_{\alpha\beta}\colon\ u_{t}+xu_{y}=|x-\alpha|^{\beta}u_{xx}, (1)

which were formally introduced in [56].11 1 The formally adjoint to the Kolmogorov forward equation ut+x​uy=(|x−α|β​u)x​xu_{t}+xu_{y}=(|x-\alpha|^{\beta}u)_{xx} is the (true) Kolmogorov backward equation −ut−x​uy=|x−α|β​ux​x-u_{t}-xu_{y}=|x-\alpha|^{\beta}u_{xx}. For convenience, we simultaneously change the signs of tt and yy, obtaining the equation (1). This change is not essential from the point of view of symmetry analysis of differential equations, and we preserve the name “Kolmogorov backward equation” for the equations of the form (1). Here α\alpha and β\beta are arbitrary real parameters. The more general Kolmogorov backward equations ut+x​uy=a⁡(x)​ux​x+b⁡(x)​uxu_{t}+xu_{y}=a(x)u_{xx}+b(x)u_{x}, appeared in [50, Eq. (30)] as models for describing the evolution of cell populations, and then only the values a=consta={\rm const} and b=0b=0 were selected as the simplest ones [50, Eq. (32)]. Equations of the form (1) with α=0\alpha=0 also arise in the course of considering path-dependent options in a constant elasticity variance environment [2, Section 5.1]. It is also shown in [2] that the Kolmogorov equations modeling the price of the geometric and arithmetic average strike call option are reduced by point transformations to the above equations, where in addition β=0\beta=0 and β=2\beta=2, respectively.

Furthermore, the equations of the form (1) are important beyond their practical applications. They also constitute a family of interesting objects for theoretical studying within the field of symmetry analysis of differential equations. The study of their symmetries provides powerful insights into the dynamics of real-world phenomena these equations model. Moreover, it offers the potential for constructing their exact solutions.

Switching to the established rigorous framework of group analysis of differential equations, the main object of the present paper is the class of differential equations of the form (1) denoted by ℱ\mathcal{F} with the tuple of arbitrary elements θ:=(α,β)\theta:=(\alpha,\beta), whose components as constants run through the solution set of the auxiliary system of differential equations αt=αx=αy=0\alpha_{t}=\alpha_{x}=\alpha_{y}=0, βt=βx=βy=0\beta_{t}=\beta_{x}=\beta_{y}=0. See [4, 7, 42, 47, 54] and references therein for the definition of classes of differential equations, a theoretical background on their transformational properties and related computational techniques. In contrast to the preliminary consideration of the class ℱ\mathcal{F} in [56], we compute the (usual) equivalence group Gℱ∼G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}} and the equivalence groupoid 𝒢ℱ∼\mathcal{G}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}} of this class and thus find out unobvious discrete equivalences between equations from ℱ\mathcal{F}. Moreover, we easily show that any equation from the class ℱ\mathcal{F} is Gℱ∼G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}}-equivalent to the equation

ℱβ′:ut+x​uy=|x|β​ux​x\displaystyle\mathcal{F}^{\prime}_{\beta}\colon\ \ u_{t}+xu_{y}=|x|^{\beta}u_{xx} (2)

with the same β\beta. The equations ℱβ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime}_{\beta} constitute the class ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime}, where β\beta remains the sole arbitrary element. The above similarity between equations from the classes ℱ\mathcal{F} and ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime} means that these classes are weakly similar [42, Definition 3]. This is why their group classifications modulo their equivalence groupoids are in fact the same, but this is not the case for the analogous classifications modulo their equivalence groups. To relate the latter classifications, we perform more thorough analysis. As a result, we solve the complete group classification problems for the classes ℱ\mathcal{F} and ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime} modulo both of the above kinds of equivalences. Developing results of [27, 29, 44], we describe other symmetry properties of equations from ℱ\mathcal{F} and construct wide families of their exact solutions in closed form. Even though the arbitrary elements of the classes ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime} and ℱ\mathcal{F} are just constant parameters, symmetry analysis of these classes and their single elements is highly nontrivial.

More specifically, we begin solving the equivalence problem for the classes ℱ\mathcal{F} and ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime} by describing properties of their equivalence groupoids 𝒢ℱ∼\mathcal{G}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}} and 𝒢ℱ′∼\mathcal{G}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}^{\prime}} in Section 2 using the advanced version of the direct method. A disadvantage of the direct method is that its straightforward application to the classes ℱ\mathcal{F} and ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime} leads to tedious and cumbersome computations. An additional complication is provided by the fact that these classes are not normalized in the usual sense. Nevertheless, the problem complexity can be reduced in the following way. We first embed the classes ℱ\mathcal{F} and ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime} in the class ℱ¯\bar{\mathcal{F}} of the linear (1+2)-dimensional second-order ultraparabolic equations of the form

ut+B⁡(t,x,y)​uy=A2​(t,x,y)​ux​x+A1​(t,x,y)​ux+A0​(t,x,y)​u+C⁡(t,x,y)withA2≠0,Bx≠0,\displaystyle\begin{split}&u_{t}+B(t,x,y)u_{y}=A^{2}(t,x,y)u_{xx}+A^{1}(t,x,y)u_{x}+A^{0}(t,x,y)u+C(t,x,y)\\ &\text{with}\quad A^{2}\neq 0,\quad B_{x}\neq 0,\end{split} (3)

which is normalized and whose equivalence pseudogroup Gℱ¯∼G^{\sim}_{\bar{\mathcal{F}}} and thus equivalence groupoid 𝒢ℱ¯∼\mathcal{G}^{\sim}_{\bar{\mathcal{F}}} are known [27, 30]. The tuple θ¯:=(B,A2,A1,A0,C)\bar{\theta}:=(B,A^{2},A^{1},A^{0},C) of arbitrary elements of the class ℱ¯\bar{\mathcal{F}} runs through the solution set of the system of the inequalities A2≠0A^{2}\neq 0 and Bx≠0B_{x}\neq 0 with no restrictions on A0A^{0}, A1A^{1} and CC. The class embeddings lead to the corresponding groupoid embeddings 𝒢ℱ∼↪𝒢ℱ¯∼{\mathcal{G}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}}\hookrightarrow\mathcal{G}^{\sim}_{\bar{\mathcal{F}}}} and 𝒢ℱ′∼↪𝒢ℱ¯∼{\mathcal{G}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}^{\prime}}\hookrightarrow\mathcal{G}^{\sim}_{\bar{\mathcal{F}}}}. We use the description of 𝒢ℱ¯∼\mathcal{G}^{\sim}_{\bar{\mathcal{F}}} to derive basic properties of the equivalence groupoids 𝒢ℱ∼\mathcal{G}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}} and 𝒢ℱ′∼\mathcal{G}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}^{\prime}} in Section 2, which allows us to simplify the computation of the equivalence groups Gℱ∼G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}} and Gℱ′∼G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}^{\prime}} and the equivalence algebras 𝔤ℱ∼\mathfrak{g}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}} and 𝔤ℱ′∼\mathfrak{g}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}^{\prime}} of the classes ℱ\mathcal{F} and ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime} in Sections 3 and 4, respectively. We show that the equivalence group Gℱ′∼G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}^{\prime}} contains the distinguished discrete equivalence transformation

𝒥′:t~=y​sgnx,x~=1x,y~=t​sgnx,u~=ux,β~=5−β,\displaystyle\mathscr{J}^{\prime}\colon\hskip 10.00002pt\tilde{t}=y\mathop{\rm sgn}\nolimits x,\hskip 10.00002pt\tilde{x}=\frac{1}{x},\hskip 10.00002pt\tilde{y}=t\mathop{\rm sgn}\nolimits x,\hskip 10.00002pt\tilde{u}=\frac{u}{x},\hskip 10.00002pt\tilde{\beta}=5-\beta, (4)

which turns out to be the only point equivalence transformation that is essential for carrying out the group classification of the class ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime}. Due to this transformation, we can impose the gauge β⩽5/2\beta\leqslant 5/2.

Remark 1.

Instead of the class ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime}, we can consider the subset of its equations, where the constant arbitrary element β\beta takes only rational values with odd denominators, and replace such equations by their counterparts without the absolute value sign,

ut+x​uy=xβ​ux​x.\displaystyle u_{t}+xu_{y}=x^{\beta}u_{xx}. (5)

Then the equivalence transformation (4) is replaced by the simpler transformation

t~=y,x~=1x,y~=t,u~=ux,β~=5−β\displaystyle\tilde{t}=y,\hskip 10.00002pt\tilde{x}=\frac{1}{x},\hskip 10.00002pt\tilde{y}=t,\hskip 10.00002pt\tilde{u}=\frac{u}{x},\hskip 10.00002pt\tilde{\beta}=5-\beta (6)

between equations of the form (5). For the specific values β=−1,1,3,5\beta=-1,1,3,5, when they are considered separately from the generic values of β\beta, we present exact solutions of the corresponding equation (5) but not (2).

In Section A, we also compute the equivalence groups Gℱ∼G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}} and Gℱ′∼G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}^{\prime}} using the automorphism-based version of the algebraic method, which was originally proposed by Hydon [20, 21, 22, 23] for finding the point symmetry groups of single systems of differential equations and extended to finding the equivalence groups of classes of such systems in [5]. This gives the first example of such computation in the literature. Since the dimensions of the corresponding equivalence algebras 𝔤ℱ∼\mathfrak{g}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}} and 𝔤ℱ′∼\mathfrak{g}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}^{\prime}} are relatively high, the straightforward construction of their automorphism groups is complicated, perhaps even impossible. To overcome this challenge, we first obtain a sufficient number of megaideals of the algebras 𝔤ℱ∼\mathfrak{g}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}} and 𝔤ℱ′∼\mathfrak{g}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}^{\prime}}, which allowed us, after fixing bases consistent with the constructed megaideal hierarchies, to preliminarily constraint automorphism matrices for proceeding with their computation in an efficient way. In total, we observe that the construction of the groups Gℱ∼G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}} and Gℱ′∼G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}^{\prime}} by the algebraic method is more involved than that by the advanced version of the direct method. Nevertheless, this serves as an excellent cross-verification of the correctness of the obtained results. In addition, to the best of our knowledge, there has been no comparison in the literature of the capabilities of these two methods when applied to a particular class of differential equations.

The results of the group classifications of the classes ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime} and ℱ\mathcal{F} are presented in Section 5. We prove that there are only two Gℱ′∼G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}^{\prime}}-inequivalent cases of essential Lie symmetry extensions in the class ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime}, with β=0\beta=0 and β=2\beta=2. The corresponding essential Lie invariance algebras 𝔤0ess\mathfrak{g}^{\rm ess}_{0} and 𝔤2ess\mathfrak{g}^{\rm ess}_{2} are eight- and five-dimensional, respectively. The essential Lie invariance algebra 𝔤βess\mathfrak{g}^{\rm ess}_{\beta} of the equation ℱβ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime}_{\beta} in the generic case, where β∈ℝ∖{0,2,3,5}\beta\in\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0,2,3,5\}, is four-dimensional and is isomorphic to the algebra A3.4a⊕A1A_{3.4}^{a}\oplus A_{1} with a=(β−2)/(β−3)a=(\beta-2)/(\beta-3) in the notation of [46]. Among these Lie algebras with β∈(−∞,5/2]∖{0,2}\beta\in(-\infty,5/2]\setminus\{0,2\}, there are no pairwise isomorphic ones. Hence the corresponding equations are definitely Gℱ′∼G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}^{\prime}}-inequivalent. The above implies that 𝒢ℱ∼\mathcal{G}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}}-equivalent cases of essential Lie symmetry extensions within the class ℱ\mathcal{F} are exhausted by the equations ℱ00\mathcal{F}_{00} and ℱ02\mathcal{F}_{02}. Due to the inconsistency of the groups Gℱ′∼G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}^{\prime}} and Gℱ∼G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}}, the classification list for the class ℱ\mathcal{F} up to the Gℱ∼G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}}-equivalence should also include the cases β=5\beta=5 and β=3\beta=3 with α=0\alpha=0, which are Gℱ′∼G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}^{\prime}}-equivalent to the cases β=0\beta=0 and β=2\beta=2, respectively.

The equations ℱ0′\mathcal{F}^{\prime}_{0} and ℱ2′\mathcal{F}^{\prime}_{2} are also singled out within the class ℱ¯\bar{\mathcal{F}} by their exceptional Lie symmetry properties. The dimension of 𝔤0ess\mathfrak{g}^{\rm ess}_{0} is maximum for the essential Lie invariance algebras of equations from this class. Moreover, the equation ℱ0′\mathcal{F}^{\prime}_{0} is the unique equation with this property in ℱ¯\bar{\mathcal{F}} modulo the point equivalence. The algebra 𝔤2ess\mathfrak{g}^{\rm ess}_{2} is five-dimensional and nonsolvable and up to the point equivalence, the equation ℱ2′\mathcal{F}^{\prime}_{2} is the unique equation in the class ℱ¯\bar{\mathcal{F}} that satisfies this property. This is why the equations ℱ0′\mathcal{F}^{\prime}_{0} and ℱ2′\mathcal{F}^{\prime}_{2} were referred to as the remarkable Fokker–Planck equation and the fine Kolmogorov backward equation, and their extended symmetry analysis was carried out in [27] and [29], respectively.

In Sections 6 and 7, we outline and complete the results of [27, 29, 44] on the equations ℱ0′\mathcal{F}^{\prime}_{0} and ℱ2′\mathcal{F}^{\prime}_{2}, including the solution generation for these equations using their recursion operators related to their Lie symmetries. We also generate new solution families of the equation ℱ2′\mathcal{F}^{\prime}_{2} using Darboux transformations of its codimension-one submodels, which are derived in Section B. All the known results on the equations ℱ0′\mathcal{F}^{\prime}_{0} and ℱ2′\mathcal{F}^{\prime}_{2} are extended to their Gℱ′∼G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}^{\prime}}-counterparts ℱ5′\mathcal{F}^{\prime}_{5} and ℱ3′\mathcal{F}^{\prime}_{3}, respectively. In particular, this provides the point symmetry pseudogroups and wide families of exact solutions of ℱ5′\mathcal{F}^{\prime}_{5} and ℱ3′\mathcal{F}^{\prime}_{3}. To be precise, we actually consider the equations of the form (5) with β=5\beta=5 and β=3\beta=3 instead of ℱ5′\mathcal{F}^{\prime}_{5} and ℱ3′\mathcal{F}^{\prime}_{3} and use the transformation (6) but not (4).

Section 8 is devoted to the extended symmetry analysis of the equations ℱβ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime}_{\beta} with β∈ℝ∖{0,2,3,5}\beta\in\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0,2,3,5\}, which constitute the case of zero essential Lie symmetry extension within the class ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime}. An original combination of the direct and algebraic methods is applied in Section 8.1 for constructing the point symmetry pseudogroups of these equations. Jointly with the obtained descriptions of the analogous pseudogroups for the other values of β\beta, β∈{0,2,3,5}\beta\in\{0,2,3,5\}, it provides the exhaustive description of the fundamental groupoid 𝒢ℱ′f\mathcal{G}^{\rm f}_{\mathcal{F}^{\prime}} of the class ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime}. Hence, combining it with results of Section 2, we obtain the complete descriptions of the equivalence groupoids 𝒢ℱ′∼\mathcal{G}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}^{\prime}} and 𝒢ℱ∼\mathcal{G}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}}, which are presented in Section 9. After listing inequivalent subalgebras of the essential Lie invariance algebra 𝔤βess\mathfrak{g}^{\rm ess}_{\beta} of the equation ℱβ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime}_{\beta} for each value of β\beta from ℝ∖{0,2,3,5}\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0,2,3,5\} in Section 8.2, we classify its Lie reductions of codimension one and two in Sections 8.3 and 8.4 up to the Gℱ′∼G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}^{\prime}}-equivalence. In the latter section, we also show that Lie reductions of codimension three do not lead to new solutions of ℱβ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime}_{\beta}. Involving the Gℱ′∼G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}^{\prime}}-equivalence allows us to reduce the number of cases to be considered. We have found hidden symmetries and constructed wide families of exact solutions of the equations ℱβ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime}_{\beta} with β∈ℝ∖{0,2,3,5}\beta\in\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0,2,3,5\} that are associated with the codimension-one Lie reductions to the linear (1+1)(1+1)-dimensional heat equations with the zero or the inverse square potentials. The most prominent among them are the solutions associated with the value β=1\beta=1 and their Gℱ′∼G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}^{\prime}}-counterparts for β=4\beta=4. Another prominent case is given by some codimension-two Lie reductions for β=−1\beta=-1 and their Gℱ′∼G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}^{\prime}}-counterparts for β=6\beta=6, which results in Whittaker equations. What is particularly surprising is that these are both the prominent cases, where constructed families of solutions can be significantly extended using the action by recursion operators of ℱβ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime}_{\beta} associated with Lie symmetries of ℱβ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime}_{\beta}, which is the subject of Section 8.5. In total, Section 8 on its own gives an exhaustive symmetry analysis of the equations ℱβ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime}_{\beta} for the generic case of β\beta.

Summarizing the results of the present paper in Section 9, we highlight discovered remarkable and surprising properties of the classes ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime} and ℱ\mathcal{F} and their single elements, emphasize novel features of our study and outline research perspectives regarding these classes as well as the superclass ℱ¯\bar{\mathcal{F}}.

For readers’ convenience, the constructed exact solutions of the equations of the form (2) are marked by the bullet symbol ∙\bullet . Given a class of differential equations, π\pi denotes the natural projection of the joint space of the variables, and the arbitrary elements onto the space of the variables only.

2 Equivalence groupoids

We first compute the equivalence groupoids and the equivalence groups of the classes ℱ\mathcal{F} and ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime} using the advanced version of the direct method. See, e.g., [25, 54] and references therein for required notions and techniques. Recall that the direct method is based on the definition of admissible transformations of a class of differential equations. Let ℒ|𝒮={ℒθ∣θ∈𝒮}\mathcal{L}|_{\mathcal{S}}=\{\mathcal{L}_{\theta}\mid\theta\in\mathcal{S}\} be a class of systems of differential equations ℒθ\mathcal{L}_{\theta} for unknown functions u=(u1,…,um)u=(u^{1},\ldots,u^{m}) of independent variables x=(x1,…,xn)x=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}) with the arbitrary-element tuple θ=(θ1,…,θk)\theta=(\theta^{1},\dots,\theta^{k}) running through the solution set 𝒮\mathcal{S} of an auxiliary system of differential equations and inequalities. Suppose that a point transformation Φ\Phi in the space with the coordinates (x,u)(x,u), Φ\Phi: x~=X⁡(x,u)\tilde{x}=X(x,u), u~=U⁡(x,u)\tilde{u}=U(x,u) with nonzero Jacobian |∂(X,U)/∂(x,u)||\partial(X,U)/\partial(x,u)|, relates systems ℒθ\mathcal{L}_{\theta} and ℒθ~\mathcal{L}_{\tilde{\theta}} from the class ℒ|𝒮\mathcal{L}|_{\mathcal{S}}, Φ∗​ℒθ=ℒθ~\Phi_{*}\mathcal{L}_{\theta}=\mathcal{L}_{\tilde{\theta}}. Expressing the required derivatives of u~\tilde{u} with respect to x~\tilde{x} in terms of the original derivatives of uu with respect to xx using the chain rule, we substitute the derived expressions into the system ℒθ~\mathcal{L}_{\tilde{\theta}}, obtaining the system (Φ−1)∗​ℒθ~(\Phi^{-1})_{*}\mathcal{L}_{\tilde{\theta}}, which should be identically satisfied on the solutions of ℒθ\mathcal{L}_{\theta}. The splitting of the obtained condition with respect to the parametric derivatives of the system ℒθ\mathcal{L}_{\theta} usually results in an overdetermined coupled system of nonlinear differential equations, which is highly difficult to solve if possible at all. However, in the particular case of the classes ℱ\mathcal{F} and ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime}, we are able to perform the computations both efficiently and elegantly using the embedding of these classes in the class ℱ¯\bar{\mathcal{F}}, which is constituted by the equations of the form (3), and the explicit description of its known equivalence groupoid. Embedding a class ℒ|𝒮\mathcal{L}|_{\mathcal{S}} in a superclass with known or easier computed equivalence groupoid for deriving principal constraints for admissible transformations within ℒ|𝒮\mathcal{L}|_{\mathcal{S}}, which simplifies the further required computations, is the essence of the advanced version of the direct method. A good choice for such a superclass is a normalized class of differential equations.

Theorem 2.

The class ℱ¯\bar{\mathcal{F}} is normalized. Its (usual) equivalence pseudogroup Gℱ¯∼G^{\sim}_{\bar{\mathcal{F}}} consists of the point transformations with the components

t~=T⁡(t,y),x~=X⁡(t,x,y),y~=Y⁡(t,y),u~=U1​(t,x,y)​u+U0​(t,x,y),\displaystyle\tilde{t}=T(t,y),\hskip 10.00002pt\tilde{x}=X(t,x,y),\hskip 10.00002pt\tilde{y}=Y(t,y),\hskip 10.00002pt\tilde{u}=U^{1}(t,x,y)u+U^{0}(t,x,y), (7a)
A~0=−U1Tt+B​Ty​E​1U1,A~1=A1​XxTt+B​Ty−Xt+B​XyTt+B​Ty+A2​Xx​x−2​Xx​Ux1/U1Tt+B​Ty,\displaystyle\tilde{A}^{0}=\frac{-U^{1}}{T_{t}+BT_{y}}E\frac{1}{U^{1}},\hskip 10.00002pt\tilde{A}^{1}=A^{1}\frac{X_{x}}{T_{t}+BT_{y}}-\frac{X_{t}+BX_{y}}{T_{t}+BT_{y}}+A^{2}\frac{X_{xx}-2X_{x}U^{1}_{x}/U^{1}}{T_{t}+BT_{y}}, (7b)
A~2=A2​Xx2Tt+B​Ty,B~=Yt+B​YyTt+B​Ty,C~=U1Tt+B​Ty​(C−E​U0U1),\displaystyle\tilde{A}^{2}=A^{2}\frac{X_{x}^{2}}{T_{t}+BT_{y}},\hskip 10.00002pt\tilde{B}=\frac{Y_{t}+BY_{y}}{T_{t}+BT_{y}},\hskip 10.00002pt\tilde{C}=\frac{U^{1}}{T_{t}+BT_{y}}\left(C-E\frac{U^{0}}{U^{1}}\right), (7c)

where TT, XX, YY, U1U^{1} and U0U^{0} are arbitrary smooth functions of their arguments with (Tt​Yy−Ty​Yt)​Xx​U1≠0(T_{t}Y_{y}-T_{y}Y_{t})X_{x}U^{1}\neq 0, and E:=∂t+B∂y−A2∂x​x−A1∂x−A0E:=\partial_{t}+B\partial_{y}-A^{2}\partial_{xx}-A^{1}\partial_{x}-A^{0}.

There are the following embeddings for ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime}, ℱ\mathcal{F} and ℱ¯\bar{\mathcal{F}} considered as sets of differential equations:

ℱ′↪ℱ↪ℱ¯.\mathcal{F}^{\prime}\hookrightarrow\mathcal{F}\hookrightarrow\bar{\mathcal{F}}.

These embeddings arise from the embeddings 𝒮ℱ′↪𝒮ℱ↪𝒮ℱ¯\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{F}^{\prime}}\hookrightarrow\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{F}}\hookrightarrow\mathcal{S}_{\bar{\mathcal{F}}} of the corresponding sets 𝒮ℱ′\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{F}^{\prime}}, 𝒮ℱ′\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{F}^{\prime}} and 𝒮ℱ¯\mathcal{S}_{\bar{\mathcal{F}}} of arbitrary elements, which are respectively defined via the mappings

𝒮ℱ′∋(β)↦(0,β)∈𝒮ℱ,𝒮ℱ∋(α,β)↦(x,0,0,0,|x−α|β)∈𝒮ℱ¯,\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{F}^{\prime}}\ni(\beta)\mapsto(0,\beta)\in\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{F}},\hskip 10.00002pt\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{F}}\ni(\alpha,\beta)\mapsto(x,0,0,0,|x-\alpha|^{\beta})\in\mathcal{S}_{\bar{\mathcal{F}}},

which can be treated as class reparameterizations. Thus, the embedding ℱ′↪ℱ¯\mathcal{F}^{\prime}\hookrightarrow\bar{\mathcal{F}} corresponds to their composition 𝒮ℱ′↪𝒮ℱ¯\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{F}^{\prime}}\hookrightarrow\mathcal{S}_{\bar{\mathcal{F}}}. The above maps also induce embeddings on the level of equivalence groupoids, 𝒢ℱ′∼↪𝒢ℱ∼↪𝒢ℱ¯∼\mathcal{G}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}^{\prime}}\hookrightarrow\mathcal{G}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}}\hookrightarrow\mathcal{G}^{\sim}_{\bar{\mathcal{F}}}.

Under the successive embeddings, the class ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime} can be considered as a subclass of ℱ\mathcal{F} and a subclass ℱ¯\bar{\mathcal{F}}, which are singled out by the additional auxiliary constraints α=0\alpha=0 and A1=A0=C=0A^{1}=A^{0}=C=0, B=xB=x, At2=Ay2=0A^{2}_{t}=A^{2}_{y}=0, (x​ln⁡|x|)​Ax2=A2​ln⁡A2(x\ln|x|)A^{2}_{x}=A^{2}\ln A^{2}, respectively. At the same time, even after the embedding ℱ↪ℱ¯\mathcal{F}\hookrightarrow\bar{\mathcal{F}}, the class ℱ\mathcal{F} cannot be interpreted as a subclass of ℱ¯\bar{\mathcal{F}} according to the formal definition of subclass given in [47] since the set of A2A^{2} of the form A2=|x−α|βA^{2}=|x-\alpha|^{\beta}, where α\alpha and β\beta are arbitrary constants, is the union of the solution sets of the systems A2=1A^{2}=1 and At2=Ay2=0A^{2}_{t}=A^{2}_{y}=0, Φx​x=−sgn(x−α)Φxexp(ΦΦx​x/Φx2)\Phi_{xx}=-\mathop{\rm sgn}\nolimits(x-\alpha)\Phi_{x}\exp\left(\Phi\Phi_{xx}/\Phi_{x}^{2}\right) with Φ=ln⁡A2\Phi=\ln A^{2} but not the solution set of a regular system of differential equations and differential inequalities. We can overcome this obstacle via extending the notion of class of differential equations by allowing arbitrary class elements to run the union of solution sets of auxiliary systems of differential equations and differential inequalities.

The aforementioned arguments allow us to use Theorem 2 in the course of computing the equivalence groupoids 𝒢ℱ∼\mathcal{G}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}} and 𝒢ℱ′∼\mathcal{G}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}^{\prime}} and the equivalence groups Gℱ∼G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}} and Gℱ′∼G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}^{\prime}} of the classes ℱ\mathcal{F} and ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime}. For this computation, the following elementary lemma is useful.

If the equality C1​|x−μ1|ν1​|x−μ2|ν2=C2​|x−μ3|ν3C_{1}|x-\mu_{1}|^{\nu_{1}}|x-\mu_{2}|^{\nu_{2}}=C_{2}|x-\mu_{3}|^{\nu_{3}} holds, where C1C_{1}, C2C_{2}, ν1\nu_{1}, ν2\nu_{2}, ν3\nu_{3}, μ1\mu_{1}, μ2\mu_{2}, μ3\mu_{3} are constants with C1​C2≠0C_{1}C_{2}\neq 0, then μ1=μ2=μ3\mu_{1}=\mu_{2}=\mu_{3} and ν3=ν1+ν2\nu_{3}=\nu_{1}+\nu_{2}, C1=C2C_{1}=C_{2}.

Theorem 4.

(i) The point transformations 𝒮⁡(c1)\mathscr{S}(c_{1}): (t~,x~,y~,u~,β~,α~)=(t,x+c1,y+c1​t,u,β,α+c1)(\tilde{t},\tilde{x},\tilde{y},\tilde{u},\tilde{\beta},\tilde{\alpha})=(t,x+c_{1},y+c_{1}t,u,\beta,\alpha+c_{1}) where c1c_{1} is arbitrary constant, constitute a one-parameter group of equivalence transformations of the class ℱ\mathcal{F}.

(ii) The wide family of admissible transformations 𝒮α​β:=((α,β),π∗​𝒮​(−α),(0,β))\mathcal{S}_{\alpha\beta}:=\big((\alpha,\beta),\pi_{*}\mathscr{S}(-\alpha),(0,\beta)\big) of the class ℱ\mathcal{F} from the action groupoid of its equivalence group maps this class onto the class ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime} interpreted as a subclass of ℱ\mathcal{F}.

(iii) The point transformation 𝒥′\mathscr{J}^{\prime} given in (4) is a (discrete) equivalence transformation of the class ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime}.

(iv) The class ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime} is semi-normalized with respect to the discrete equivalence subgroup generated by 𝒥′\mathscr{J}^{\prime}. In other words, the equivalence groupoid 𝒢ℱ′∼\mathcal{G}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}^{\prime}} of ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime} is the Frobenius product of the action groupoid of this subgroup and the fundamental equivalence groupoid 𝒢ℱ′f\mathcal{G}^{\rm f}_{\mathcal{F}^{\prime}} of ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime}.

Proof.

Since items (i)–(iii) are straightforwardly verified, except the discreteness of 𝒥′\mathscr{J}^{\prime}, which follows from item (iv), it suffices to prove only item (iv).

The determining equations for admissible transformations of the class ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime} can be derived by restricting their counterparts for the class ℱ¯\bar{\mathcal{F}} in view of the embedding ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime} in ℱ¯\bar{\mathcal{F}}. Corollary 5.

(i) Different equations ℱβ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime}_{\beta} and ℱβ~′\mathcal{F}^{\prime}_{\tilde{\beta}} are similar with respect to point transformations if and only if β+β~=5\beta+\tilde{\beta}=5.

(iii) The equivalence groupoid 𝒢ℱ∼\mathcal{G}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}} of ℱ\mathcal{F} is generated by admissible transformations 𝒮α​β\mathcal{S}_{\alpha\beta} and elements of 𝒢ℱ′∼\mathcal{G}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}^{\prime}}. More specifically, for each admissible transformation ((α,β),Φ,(α~,β~))\big((\alpha,\beta),\Phi,(\tilde{\alpha},\tilde{\beta})\big) of ℱ\mathcal{F}, we have Φ=π∗​𝒮​(α~)∘Φ˘∘π∗​𝒮​(−α)\Phi=\pi_{*}\mathscr{S}(\tilde{\alpha})\circ\breve{\Phi}\circ\pi_{*}\mathscr{S}(-\alpha) for some point transformation Φ˘\breve{\Phi} with (β,Φ˘,β~)∈𝒢ℱ′∼(\beta,\breve{\Phi},\tilde{\beta})\in\mathcal{G}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}^{\prime}}.

3 Equivalence group and equivalence algebra
of the original class

We compute the equivalence group of the class ℱ\mathcal{F} of Kolmogorov backward equations with power diffusivity using two fundamentally different approaches, the direct method in this section and the algebraic method in Section A.1. While each of them has its advantages and drawbacks as well as its scope of applicability, they complement each other and provide a robust cross-verification of the correctness of computations when used in conjunction. Moreover, in the literature, no one has compared the capabilities of these two methods when applied to constructing the equivalence group of a specific class; see [6] for a similar comparison in the case of computing the point symmetry group of a single system of differential equation. The class ℱ\mathcal{F} can serve as an excellent instructive example for this particular purpose.

Theorem 6.

The equivalence group Gℱ∼G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}} consists of the point transformations

t~=t+c0,x~=ϵx+c1,y~=ϵy+c1t+c2,u~=c3u+c4(tx−y)+c5x+c6,α~=ϵα+c1,β~=β,\displaystyle\begin{split}&\tilde{t}=t+c_{0},\quad\tilde{x}=\epsilon x+c_{1},\quad\tilde{y}=\epsilon y+c_{1}t+c_{2},\quad\tilde{u}=c_{3}u+c_{4}(tx-y)+c_{5}x+c_{6},\\ &\tilde{\alpha}=\epsilon\alpha+c_{1},\quad\tilde{\beta}=\beta,\end{split} (10)

where ϵ=±1\epsilon=\pm 1, c0c_{0}, …, c6c_{6} are arbitrary constants with c3≠0c_{3}\neq 0.

Proof.

We apply the advanced version of the direct method. In view of the embedding ℱ↪ℱ¯\mathcal{F}\hookrightarrow\bar{\mathcal{F}}, the transformational parts of admissible transformations of the class ℱ\mathcal{F} takes the form (7a), where the involved parameter functions satisfy the equations (7b) and (7c) specified for this class as a subclass of ℱ¯\bar{\mathcal{F}},

In view of item (ii) of Corollary 5, we have at most two cases for the β\beta-components of equivalence transformation of ℱ\mathcal{F}, β~=β\tilde{\beta}=\beta and β~=5−β\tilde{\beta}=5-\beta. Differentiating the last equation with respect to yy and splitting the result with respect to α\alpha, we obtain Yt​y=Yy​y=0Y_{ty}=Y_{yy}=0. Therefore, T=t+c0T=t+c_{0}, Y=ϵ​y+c1​t+c2Y=\epsilon y+c_{1}t+c_{2}, and thus X=ϵ​x+c1X=\epsilon x+c_{1} for some constants c0c_{0}, c1c_{1} and c2c_{2}. Remark 7.

The transformations of the form (10) with ϵ=1\epsilon=1 and c1=0c_{1}=0 constitute a normal subgroup G^ℱ∩\hat{G}^{\cap}_{\mathcal{F}} of Gℱ∼G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}}, which is isomorphic, via the natural projection onto the space ℝt,x,y,u4\mathbb{R}^{4}_{t,x,y,u}, to the kernel point symmetry group Gℱ∩G^{\cap}_{\mathcal{F}} of the class ℱ\mathcal{F}, cf. [14, Proposition 3]. The quotient of Gℱ∼G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}} with respect to G^ℱ∩\hat{G}^{\cap}_{\mathcal{F}} is isomorphic to the group ℝ×ℤ2\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{Z}_{2} and can be naturally identified with the subgroup of Gℱ′∼G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}^{\prime}} that is generated by the transformations 𝒥′\mathscr{J}^{\prime} and

𝒮⁡(c1):t~=t,x~=ϵ​x+c1,y~=ϵ​y+c1​t,u~=u,α~=ϵ​α+c1,β~=β.\displaystyle\mathscr{S}(c_{1})\colon\hskip 10.00002pt\tilde{t}=t,\hskip 10.00002pt\tilde{x}=\epsilon x+c_{1},\hskip 10.00002pt\tilde{y}=\epsilon y+c_{1}t,\hskip 10.00002pt\tilde{u}=u,\hskip 10.00002pt\tilde{\alpha}=\epsilon\alpha+c_{1},\hskip 10.00002pt\tilde{\beta}=\beta.

Hence, these transformations can be considered as the only essential equivalence transformations within the class ℱ\mathcal{F}, which establish relations between different elements of ℱ\mathcal{F}.

Knowing the equivalence group Gℱ∼G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}} of the class ℱ\mathcal{F}, we can easily construct the equivalence algebra 𝔤ℱ∼\mathfrak{g}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}} of this class as the set of generators of one-parameter subgroups of Gℱ∼G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}}.

Corollary 8.

The equivalence algebra 𝔤ℱ∼\mathfrak{g}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}} of the class ℱ\mathcal{F} is spanned by the vector fields ∂t\partial_{t}, ∂x+t∂y+∂α\partial_{x}+t\partial_{y}+\partial_{\alpha}, ∂y\partial_{y}, u∂uu\partial_{u}, (tx−y)∂u(tx-y)\partial_{u}, x∂ux\partial_{u} and ∂u\partial_{u}.

Corollary 9.

The usual equivalence group Gℱ∼G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}} of the class ℱ\mathcal{F} is generated by the one-parameter groups associated with the basis vector fields of the equivalence algebra 𝔤ℱ∼\mathfrak{g}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}} of this class and its two discrete equivalence transformations,

ℐu:(t,x,y,u,α,β)↦(t,x,y,−u,α,β)andℐs:(t,x,y,u,α,β)↦(t,−x,−y,u,−α,β).\displaystyle\mathscr{I}_{u}\colon(t,x,y,u,\alpha,\beta)\mapsto(t,x,y,-u,\alpha,\beta)\hskip 10.00002pt\mbox{and}\hskip 10.00002pt\mathscr{I}_{\rm s}\colon(t,x,y,u,\alpha,\beta)\mapsto(t,-x,-y,u,-\alpha,\beta).

The algebra 𝔤ℱ∼\mathfrak{g}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}} can be represented as the semidirect sum 𝔤ℱ∼=⟨∂t+t∂y+∂α⟩  ∈𝔤^ℱ∩\mathfrak{g}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}}=\langle\partial_{t}+t\partial_{y}+\partial_{\alpha}\rangle\mathbin{\mbox{$\hbox to0.0pt{$\displaystyle\hskip 3.31528pt\rule{0.4pt}{5.16663pt}$\hss}{\in}$}}\hat{\mathfrak{g}}^{\cap}_{\mathcal{F}}, where the ideal 𝔤^ℱ∩\hat{\mathfrak{g}}^{\cap}_{\mathcal{F}} spanned by the vector fields ∂t\partial_{t}, ∂y\partial_{y}, u∂uu\partial_{u}, (tx−y)∂u(tx-y)\partial_{u}, x∂ux\partial_{u} and ∂u\partial_{u} is isomorphic to the kernel invariance algebra 𝔤ℱ∩\mathfrak{g}^{\cap}_{\mathcal{F}} of equations from the class ℱ\mathcal{F}, see Corollary 17. Both the algebras 𝔤ℱ∼\mathfrak{g}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}} and 𝔤^ℱ∩\hat{\mathfrak{g}}^{\cap}_{\mathcal{F}} are indecomposable, two-step solvable and not nilpotent. The nilradicals of the algebras 𝔤ℱ∼\mathfrak{g}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}} and 𝔤^ℱ∩\hat{\mathfrak{g}}^{\cap}_{\mathcal{F}} respectively are

𝔫ℱ∼=⟨∂x+t∂y+∂α,∂t,∂y,(tx−y)∂u,x∂u,∂u⟩and𝔫ℱ∩=⟨∂t,∂y,(tx−y)∂u,x∂u,∂u⟩.\mathfrak{n}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}}=\langle\partial_{x}+t\partial_{y}+\partial_{\alpha},\partial_{t},\partial_{y},(tx-y)\partial_{u},x\partial_{u},\partial_{u}\rangle\hskip 10.00002pt\mbox{and}\hskip 10.00002pt\mathfrak{n}^{\cap}_{\mathcal{F}}=\langle\partial_{t},\partial_{y},(tx-y)\partial_{u},x\partial_{u},\partial_{u}\rangle.

The nilradical 𝔫ℱ∩\mathfrak{n}^{\cap}_{\mathcal{F}} and the algebra 𝔤^ℱ∩\hat{\mathfrak{g}}^{\cap}_{\mathcal{F}} are isomorphic to the nilpotent algebra L51L_{5}^{1} [36] (or g5.1\mathrm{g}_{5.1} in the notation of [38]) and the solvable algebra g6.54g_{6.54} with λ=γ=1\lambda=\gamma=1 [39], respectively. The nilradical 𝔫ℱ∼\mathfrak{n}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}} is indecomposable and six-dimensional with the four-dimensional maximal abelian ideal ⟨∂u,x∂u,∂t,∂y⟩\langle\partial_{u},x\partial_{u},\partial_{t},\partial_{y}\rangle and the one-dimensional center ⟨∂u⟩\langle\partial_{u}\rangle. The lower central series of 𝔫ℱ∼\mathfrak{n}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}} is 𝔫ℱ∼⊃⟨∂u,x∂u,∂y⟩⊃⟨∂u⟩\mathfrak{n}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}}\supset\langle\partial_{u},x\partial_{u},\partial_{y}\rangle\supset\langle\partial_{u}\rangle. These structural properties of the algebra 𝔫ℱ∼\mathfrak{n}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}} help us to identify it. It is isomorphic to the algebra B.14 with γ=−1\gamma=-1 from Morozov’s classification of six-dimensional nilpotent algebras [36].

4 Equivalence group and equivalence algebra of the gauged class

The elements of the group Gℱ∼G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}} that preserve the subclass ℱ0\mathcal{F}_{0} constitute a proper subgroup HH of Gℱ∼G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}}. Let ϖ\varpi denote the natural projection from the space with coordinates (t,x,y,u,α,β)(t,x,y,u,\alpha,\beta) onto the space with coordinates (t,x,y,u,β)(t,x,y,u,\beta). The pushforward ϖ∗​H\varpi_{*}H of the group HH by ϖ\varpi is a subgroup of Gℱ′∼G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}^{\prime}}. Nonetheless, since the class ℱ\mathcal{F} is not normalized, we cannot guarantee that ϖ∗​H=Gℱ′∼\varpi_{*}H=G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}^{\prime}}. Moreover, we prove that ϖ∗​H⊊Gℱ′∼\varpi_{*}H\subsetneq G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}^{\prime}}. We cannot also use the embedding of the groupoid 𝒢ℱ′∼\mathcal{G}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}^{\prime}} in the groupoid 𝒢ℱ∼\mathcal{G}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}} induced by the embedding of ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime} in ℱ\mathcal{F} since the description of 𝒢ℱ∼\mathcal{G}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}} in Corollary 5(iii) is based on that of 𝒢ℱ′∼\mathcal{G}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}^{\prime}}. This is why we proceed with computing the equivalence group Gℱ′∼G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}^{\prime}} similarly to as it is done in Section 3. We apply the advanced version of the direct method to the class ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime}, which is based on the embedding of the groupoid 𝒢ℱ′∼\mathcal{G}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}^{\prime}} in the groupoid 𝒢ℱ¯∼\mathcal{G}^{\sim}_{\bar{\mathcal{F}}}; see Section A.2 for the same computation using the algebraic method.

Theorem 10.

The usual equivalence group22 2 Formally, the set of transformations Gℱ′∼G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}^{\prime}} together with the standard transformation composition form a pseudogroup rather than a group, see [29, Section A] for details. However, Gℱ′∼G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}^{\prime}} can be turned into a group in a simple way following the approach from [27, 28, 29]. It is clear that the composition of two transformations of the form (13) is also of this form and its natural domain is the entire space ℝ5:=ℝt,x,y,u,β5\mathbb{R}^{5}:=\mathbb{R}^{5}_{t,x,y,u,\beta}. Similarly, composing (13) with (14) results in a transformation of the form (14) with the natural domain ℝ5∖M0\mathbb{R}^{5}\setminus M_{0}, where M0⊂ℝ5M_{0}\subset\mathbb{R}^{5} is the hyperplane defined by the equation x=0x=0. However, the composition of two transformations of the form (14) is of the form (13) and its domain is the set ℝ5∖M0\mathbb{R}^{5}\setminus M_{0}. We can modify this operation as follows: Φ1∘modΦ2=Φ1∘Φ2\Phi_{1}\circ^{\rm mod}\Phi_{2}=\Phi_{1}\circ\Phi_{2} if Φ1\Phi_{1} and Φ2\Phi_{2} are both of the form (13) or of the forms (13) and (14). In this way, the set Gℱ′∼G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}^{\prime}} is a group with the modified composition ∘mod\circ^{\rm mod}. Gℱ′∼G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}^{\prime}} of the class ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime} consists of the transformations of the following two forms:

t~=t+c0,x~=ϵ​x,y~=ϵ​y+c1,u~=c2​u+c3​(t​x−y)+c4​x+c5,β~=β,\displaystyle\tilde{t}=t+c_{0},\ \ \tilde{x}=\epsilon x,\ \ \tilde{y}=\epsilon y+c_{1},\ \ \tilde{u}=c_{2}u+c_{3}(tx-y)+c_{4}x+c_{5},\ \ \tilde{\beta}=\beta, (13)

with Tt>0T_{t}>0. Its second and fourth equations further split with respect to β\beta to Tt=|Yy|=1T_{t}=|Y_{y}|=1, Ux​x0=0U^{0}_{xx}=0 and Ut0+x​Uy0=0U^{0}_{t}+xU^{0}_{y}=0. Remark 11.

The transformations of the form (13) constitute a normal subgroup G^ℱ′∩\hat{G}^{\cap}_{\mathcal{F}^{\prime}} of Gℱ′∼G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}^{\prime}}, which is isomorphic, via the natural projection to the space ℝt,x,y,u4\mathbb{R}^{4}_{t,x,y,u}, to the kernel point symmetry group Gℱ′∩G^{\cap}_{\mathcal{F}^{\prime}} of the class ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime}, cf. [14]. The quotient of Gℱ′∼G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}^{\prime}} with respect to G^ℱ′∩\hat{G}^{\cap}_{\mathcal{F}^{\prime}} is isomorphic to ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} and can be naturally identified with the subgroup of Gℱ′∼G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}^{\prime}} constituted by the identity transformation of (t,x,y,u,β)(t,x,y,u,\beta) and the transformation (4). Hence the latter transformation can be considered as the only essential equivalence transformation within the class ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime}, which establishes a relation between different elements of ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime}.

Modulo Gℱ′∼G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}^{\prime}}-equivalence, it suffices to consider a single value of β\beta in each pair (β1,β2)(\beta_{1},\beta_{2}) with β1+β2=5\beta_{1}+\beta_{2}=5. As the canonical representative of such a pair, we choose the value β∈(−∞,5/2]\beta\in(-\infty,5/2].

The usual equivalence group Gℱ′∼G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}^{\prime}} of the class ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime} is generated by the one-parameter groups associated with the basis vector fields of the equivalence algebra 𝔤ℱ′∼\mathfrak{g}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}^{\prime}} of this class and its discrete equivalence transformations

The quotient group of the group Gℱ′∼G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}^{\prime}} with respect to its identity component is isomorphic to the degree-four dihedral group D4\mathrm{D}_{4}. As the canonical subgroup of discrete equivalence transformations, one can take those generated by ℐu′\mathscr{I}^{\prime}_{u}, ℐs′\mathscr{I}^{\prime}_{\rm s} and 𝒥′\mathscr{J}^{\prime}, and a minimal set of generators is {ℐu′,ℐs′∘𝒥′}\{\mathscr{I}^{\prime}_{u},\,\mathscr{I}^{\prime}_{\rm s}\circ\mathscr{J}^{\prime}\}.

By π\pi we denote the natural projection of the group Gℱ′∼G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}^{\prime}} onto the quotient group of this group by its identity component. It is clear that the kernel invariance algebras 𝔤ℱ∩\mathfrak{g}^{\cap}_{\mathcal{F}} and 𝔤ℱ′∩\mathfrak{g}^{\cap}_{\mathcal{F}^{\prime}} of equations from the classes ℱ\mathcal{F} and ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime}, respectively, coincide, see Theorem 16 and Corollary 17 below. At the same time, the corresponding kernel point symmetry groups Gℱ∩G^{\cap}_{\mathcal{F}} and Gℱ′∩G^{\cap}_{\mathcal{F}^{\prime}} are different, Gℱ∩⊊Gℱ′∩G^{\cap}_{\mathcal{F}}\varsubsetneq G^{\cap}_{\mathcal{F}^{\prime}}. 5 Classification of Lie symmetries

In view of Corollary 5, the 𝒢ℱ∼\mathcal{G}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}}- and 𝒢ℱ′∼\mathcal{G}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}^{\prime}}-equivalences within the classes ℱ\mathcal{F} and ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime}, respectively, are consistent. More specifically, the equations from the class ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime} are 𝒢ℱ′∼\mathcal{G}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}^{\prime}}-equivalent if and only if their counterparts in ℱ\mathcal{F} under the embedding ℱ′↪ℱ\mathcal{F}^{\prime}\hookrightarrow\mathcal{F} are 𝒢ℱ∼\mathcal{G}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}}-equivalent. The class ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime} is semi-normalized in the usual sense, i.e., the 𝒢ℱ′∼\mathcal{G}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}^{\prime}}-equivalence coincide with the Gℱ′∼G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}^{\prime}}-equivalence. This is why it is convenient to first carry out the group classification of the class ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime} and then apply Corollary 5, Theorem 6 and Remark 11 to the obtained results for solving the group classification problem for the class ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime}.

According to the classical Lie algorithm of computing continuous point symmetries [8, 9, 40], a Lie symmetry vector field QQ of the equation ℱβ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime}_{\beta} takes the general form

Q=τ(t,x,y,u)∂t+ξx(t,x,y,u)∂x+ξy(t,x,y,u)∂y+η(t,x,y,u)∂uQ=\tau(t,x,y,u)\partial_{t}+\xi^{x}(t,x,y,u)\partial_{x}+\xi^{y}(t,x,y,u)\partial_{y}+\eta(t,x,y,u)\partial_{u}

with components that can be found from the infinitesimal invariance criterion

Q(2)​(ut+x​uy−|x|β​ux​x)|ℱβ′=(ηt+x​ηy+ξx​uy−|x|β​ηx​x−β​ξx​x−1​|x|β​ux​x)|ℱβ′=0.\displaystyle Q_{(2)}\big(u_{t}+xu_{y}-|x|^{\beta}u_{xx}\big)\big|_{\mathcal{F}^{\prime}_{\beta}}=\big(\eta^{t}+x\eta^{y}+\xi^{x}u_{y}-|x|^{\beta}\eta^{xx}-\beta\xi^{x}x^{-1}|x|^{\beta}u_{xx}\big)\big|_{\mathcal{F}^{\prime}_{\beta}}=0.

Unlike the group classification in [56], we carry out the group classification of the class ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime} up to the Gℱ′∼G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}^{\prime}}-equivalence, which coincides with the 𝒢ℱ′∼\mathcal{G}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}^{\prime}}-equivalence in view of the semi-normalization of this class. In other words, without loss of generality we can impose the gauge β⩽5/2\beta\leqslant 5/2, which in its turn reduces the number of cases we need to consider.

Theorem 16.

The kernel Lie invariance algebra 𝔤ℱ′∩\mathfrak{g}^{\cap}_{\mathcal{F}^{\prime}} of the equations from the class ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime} is

where the parameter function fβ=fβ​(t,x,y)f^{\beta}=f^{\beta}(t,x,y) runs through the solution set of this equation, and β∈(−∞,5/2]\beta\in(-\infty,5/2] modulo the Gℱ′∼G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}^{\prime}}-equivalence. the maximal Lie invariance algebra 𝔤β\mathfrak{g}_{\beta} of the equation ℱβ\mathcal{F}_{\beta} coincides with 𝔤βgen\mathfrak{g}^{\rm gen}_{\beta} if and only if β∈ℝ∖{0,2,3,5}\beta\in\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0,2,3,5\}. Proof.

Splitting the system of determining equations (15) with respect to the arbitrary element β\beta, we find the kernel Lie invariance algebra 𝔤ℱ′∩\mathfrak{g}^{\cap}_{\mathcal{F}^{\prime}} of the equations from the class ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime}.

To find the algebra 𝔤β\mathfrak{g}_{\beta}, we start with solving the system of the equations (15a) together with the fourth equation from (15b), obtaining

τ=τ⁡(t,y),ξx=−x2​τy+x​ξyy−x​τt+ξty,ξy=ξy​(t,y),η=η1​(t,x,y)​u+η0​(t,x,y),\displaystyle\tau=\tau(t,y),\hskip 10.00002pt\xi^{x}=-x^{2}\tau_{y}+x\xi^{y}_{y}-x\tau_{t}+\xi^{y}_{t},\hskip 10.00002pt\xi^{y}=\xi^{y}(t,y),\hskip 10.00002pt\eta=\eta^{1}(t,x,y)u+\eta^{0}(t,x,y),

The equivalence transformation (4) reduces the cases β=5\beta=5 and β=3\beta=3 to the cases β=0\beta=0 and β=2\beta=2, respectively. Solving the determining equations for the latter two cases results in the algebras 𝔤0\mathfrak{g}_{0} and 𝔤2\mathfrak{g}_{2}. ∎

For any β\beta, the vector fields 𝒵⁡(fβ)\mathcal{Z}(f^{\beta}) constitute the infinite-dimensional abelian ideal 𝔤βlin\mathfrak{g}^{\rm lin}_{\beta} of 𝔤β\mathfrak{g}_{\beta} that is associated with the linear superposition of solutions of ℱβ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime}_{\beta}, 𝔤βlin:={𝒵⁡(fβ)}\mathfrak{g}^{\rm lin}_{\beta}:=\{\mathcal{Z}(f^{\beta})\}. Theorems 4 and 16 and Corollary 5 jointly imply the solution of the group classification problem for the class ℱ\mathcal{F}.

Corollary 17.

The kernel Lie invariance algebra 𝔤ℱ∩\mathfrak{g}^{\cap}_{\mathcal{F}} of the equations from the class ℱ\mathcal{F} coincides with that for the class ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime}, 𝔤ℱ∩=𝔤ℱ′∩\mathfrak{g}^{\cap}_{\mathcal{F}}=\mathfrak{g}^{\cap}_{\mathcal{F}^{\prime}}. 6 Remarkable Fokker–Planck equation and its counterpart

The equation ℱ0′\mathcal{F}^{\prime}_{0} is of the simplest form among the equations from the classes ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime}, ℱ\mathcal{F} and even ℱ¯\bar{\mathcal{F}},

ℱ0′:ut+x​uy=ux​x,\displaystyle\mathcal{F}^{\prime}_{0}\colon\hskip 10.00002ptu_{t}+xu_{y}=u_{xx}, (16)

and its essential Lie invariance algebra is of the greatest dimension, which is equal to eight. Moreover, up to the equivalence with respect to point transformations, this is a unique equation with the above property within each of the above classes. This is why in [27] we called it the remarkable (1+2)-dimensional Fokker–Planck equation. We briefly review the results of [27, 44] on this equation and then extend them to the equation (5) with β=5\beta=5 using the point transformation (6).

The maximal Lie invariance algebra of the equation (16) is (see, e.g., [31])

𝔤0:=⟨𝒫t,𝒟,𝒦,𝒫3,𝒫2,𝒫1,𝒫0,ℐ,𝒵⁡(f)⟩,\displaystyle\mathfrak{g}_{0}:=\langle\mathcal{P}^{t},\,\mathcal{D},\,\mathcal{K},\,\mathcal{P}^{3},\,\mathcal{P}^{2},\,\mathcal{P}^{1},\,\mathcal{P}^{0},\,\mathcal{I},\mathcal{Z}(f)\rangle,

where

𝒫3=3t2∂x+t3∂y+3(y−tx)u∂u,𝒫2=2t∂x+t2∂y−xu∂u,𝒫1=∂x+t∂y,𝒫0=∂y,\displaystyle\mathcal{P}^{3}=3t^{2}\partial_{x}+t^{3}\partial_{y}+3(y-tx)u\partial_{u},\ \ \mathcal{P}^{2}=2t\partial_{x}+t^{2}\partial_{y}-xu\partial_{u},\ \ \mathcal{P}^{1}=\partial_{x}+t\partial_{y},\ \ \mathcal{P}^{0}=\partial_{y},
ℐ=u∂u,𝒵(f)=f(t,x,y)∂u.\displaystyle\mathcal{I}=u\partial_{u},\hskip 10.00002pt\mathcal{Z}(f)=f(t,x,y)\partial_{u}.

Here the parameter function ff runs through the solution set of the equation (16). The essential Lie invariance algebra 𝔤0ess\mathfrak{g}_{0}^{\rm ess} splits over its radical 𝔯0=⟨𝒫3,𝒫2,𝒫1,𝒫0,ℐ⟩\mathfrak{r}_{0}=\langle\mathcal{P}^{3},\mathcal{P}^{2},\mathcal{P}^{1},\mathcal{P}^{0},\mathcal{I}\rangle, which is isomorphic to the real rank-two Heisenberg algebra h⁡(2,ℝ){\rm h}(2,\mathbb{R}), 𝔤0ess=𝔣0  ∈𝔯0\mathfrak{g}_{0}^{\rm ess}=\mathfrak{f}_{0}\mathbin{\mbox{$\hbox to0.0pt{$\displaystyle\hskip 3.31528pt\rule{0.4pt}{5.16663pt}$\hss}{\in}$}}\mathfrak{r}_{0}, where 𝔣0=⟨𝒫t,𝒟,𝒦⟩\mathfrak{f}_{0}=\langle\mathcal{P}^{t},\mathcal{D},\mathcal{K}\rangle is a Levi factor of 𝔤0ess\mathfrak{g}_{0}^{\rm ess} and it is isomorphic to the real order-two special linear Lie algebra sl⁡(2,ℝ){\rm sl}(2,\mathbb{R}).

The algebra of generalized symmetries of the equation (16) was computed in [44]. The properties of the associative algebra of differential recursion operators of (16) played the key role in that computation. Moreover, these operators were applied therein to generating new solutions of ℱ0\mathcal{F}_{0} from known ones. In particular, using the solution families (19)–(22) of the Lie-invariant solutions as seed ones, large families of essentially new solutions of (16) were generated.

More specifically, consider the operators in total derivatives that are associated with the Lie-symmetry vector fields −𝒫3-\mathcal{P}^{3}, −𝒫2-\mathcal{P}^{2}, −𝒫1-\mathcal{P}^{1}, −𝒫0-\mathcal{P}^{0} and −𝒫t-\mathcal{P}^{t}, −𝒟-\mathcal{D}, −𝒦-\mathcal{K} of (16),

P^t:=(P1)2−P2​P0=Dx2−x​Dy,\displaystyle\hat{\mathrm{P}}^{t}:=(\mathrm{P}^{1})^{2}-\mathrm{P}^{2}\mathrm{P}^{0}=\mathrm{D}_{x}^{2}-x\mathrm{D}_{y},

of the associative algebra Υ𝔯0\Upsilon_{\mathfrak{r}_{0}}, respectively, and thus they are inessential in the course of generating solutions. 7 Fine Kolmogorov backward equation and its counterpart

Another distinguished equation within the classes ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime}, ℱ\mathcal{F} and ℱ¯\bar{\mathcal{F}} is the Kolmogorov backward equation ℱ2′\mathcal{F}^{\prime}_{2},

ℱ2′:ut+x​uy=x2​ux​x.\displaystyle\mathcal{F}^{\prime}_{2}\colon\hskip 10.00002ptu_{t}+xu_{y}=x^{2}u_{xx}. (24)

Its essential Lie invariance algebra is five-dimensional and nonsolvable, and modulo the point equivalence, it is the only equation from the above classes with this property. This is why in [29], we refer to ℱ2′\mathcal{F}^{\prime}_{2} as to the fine Kolmogorov backward equation. Some of the results from [29] are reviewed below.

The maximal Lie invariance algebra 𝔤2\mathfrak{g}_{2} of (24) is spanned by the vector fields

𝒫y=∂y,𝒟=x∂x+y∂y,𝒦=2xy∂x+y2∂y−ux∂u,\displaystyle\mathcal{P}^{y}=\partial_{y},\hskip 10.00002pt\mathcal{D}=x\partial_{x}+y\partial_{y},\hskip 10.00002pt\mathcal{K}=2xy\partial_{x}+y^{2}\partial_{y}-ux\partial_{u},
𝒫t=∂t,ℐ=u∂u,𝒵(f)=f(t,x,y)∂u,\displaystyle\mathcal{P}^{t}=\partial_{t},\hskip 10.00002pt\mathcal{I}=u\partial_{u},\hskip 10.00002pt\mathcal{Z}(f)=f(t,x,y)\partial_{u},

where the parameter function ff ranges through the solution set of (24).

Theorem 23 ([29]).

The point symmetry pseudogroup G2G_{2} of the fine Kolmogorov backward equation (24) consists of the point transformations of the form

t~=t+λ,x~=α​δ−β​γ(γ​y+δ)2x,y~=α​y+βγ​y+δ,u~=σ​exp⁡(−γ​xγ​y+δ)​(u+f⁡(t,x,y))\displaystyle\begin{split}&\tilde{t}=t+\lambda,\quad\tilde{x}=\frac{\alpha\delta-\beta\gamma}{(\gamma y+\delta)^{2}}x,\quad\tilde{y}=\frac{\alpha y+\beta}{\gamma y+\delta},\\[4.30554pt] &\tilde{u}=\sigma\exp\left(-\frac{\gamma x}{\gamma y+\delta}\right)\big(u+f(t,x,y)\big)\end{split}

where α\alpha, β\beta, γ\gamma and δ\delta are arbitrary constants with α​δ−β​γ=±1\alpha\delta-\beta\gamma=\pm 1 that are defined up to simultaneously alternating their signs; λ\lambda and σ\sigma are arbitrary constants with σ≠0\sigma\neq 0, and ff is an arbitrary solution of the equation (24).

Given an arbitrary seed solution u=h⁡(t,x,y)u=h(t,x,y) of (24), an element of the group G2G_{2} represented in the notation of Theorem 23 maps it to the solution

u~=σ​exp⁡(−γ​xα−γ​y)​h​(t−λ,α​δ−β​γ(α−γ​y)2​x,δ​y−βα−γ​y)+f⁡(t,x,y).\displaystyle\tilde{u}=\sigma\exp\left(-\frac{\gamma x}{\alpha-\gamma y}\right)h\left(t-\lambda,\frac{\alpha\delta-\beta\gamma}{(\alpha-\gamma y)^{2}}x,\frac{\delta y-\beta}{\alpha-\gamma y}\right)+f(t,x,y).

∙β=2:u=eμ​t|x|1/4ϑ4​μ+34(εy,2|x|)withε:=sgnx,\displaystyle\hskip-15.00003pt\bullet\hskip 10.00002pt\beta=2\colon\hskip 10.00002ptu={\rm e}^{\mu t}|x|^{1/4}\vartheta^{4\mu+\frac{3}{4}}(\varepsilon y,2\sqrt{|x|})\hskip 10.00002pt\mbox{with}\hskip 10.00002pt\varepsilon:=\mathop{\rm sgn}\nolimits x,

Moreover, this is the only nontrivial case of generating new solutions of (24) by acting Lie-symmetry operators.

Following Remark 1, instead of ℱ3′\mathcal{F}^{\prime}_{3} and the equivalence transformation (4), we can consider the equation

ut+x​uy=x3​ux​x\displaystyle u_{t}+xu_{y}=x^{3}u_{xx} (25)

Proposition 24.

The maximal Lie invariance algebra 𝔤3\mathfrak{g}_{3} of the equation (25) is spanned by the vector fields

where the parameter function ff runs through the solution set of the equation (25).

Theorem 25.

The point symmetry pseudogroup G3G_{3} of the equation (25) consists of the point transformations of the form

t~=α​t+βγ​t+δ,x~=(γ​t+δ)2α​δ−β​γx,y~=y+λ,u~=σ​(γ​t+δ)2α​δ−β​γ​exp⁡(−γ​x−1γ​t+δ)​(u+f⁡(t,x,y)),\displaystyle\begin{split}&\tilde{t}=\frac{\alpha t+\beta}{\gamma t+\delta},\quad\tilde{x}=\frac{(\gamma t+\delta)^{2}}{\alpha\delta-\beta\gamma}x,\quad\tilde{y}=y+\lambda,\\[4.30554pt] &\tilde{u}=\sigma\frac{(\gamma t+\delta)^{2}}{\alpha\delta-\beta\gamma}\exp\left(-\frac{\gamma x^{-1}}{\gamma t+\delta}\right)\big(u+f(t,x,y)\big),\end{split} (26)

8 Generic case

As the generic case, we consider the case β≠0,2,3,5\beta\neq 0,2,3,5. In view of Remark 12, up to the Gℱ′∼G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}^{\prime}}-equivalence, it suffices to consider only the equations

ℱβ′:ut+xuy=|x|βux​x,β∈(−∞,5/2]∖{0,2}.\displaystyle\mathcal{F}^{\prime}_{\beta}\colon\hskip 10.00002ptu_{t}+xu_{y}=|x|^{\beta}u_{xx},\hskip 10.00002pt\beta\in(-\infty,5/2]\setminus\{0,2\}.

According to Section 5, the essential Lie invariance algebra 𝔤βess\mathfrak{g}^{\rm ess}_{\beta} of the equation ℱβ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime}_{\beta} with such a value of β\beta is spanned by the vector fields

𝒫t:=∂t,𝒫y:=∂y,𝒟β:=(2−β)t∂t+x∂x+(3−β)y∂y,ℐ:=u∂u.\displaystyle\mathcal{P}^{t}:=\partial_{t},\hskip 10.00002pt\mathcal{P}^{y}:=\partial_{y},\hskip 10.00002pt\mathcal{D}^{\beta}:=(2-\beta)t\partial_{t}+x\partial_{x}+(3-\beta)y\partial_{y},\hskip 10.00002pt\mathcal{I}:=u\partial_{u}.

Up to the skew-symmetry of the Lie bracket of vector fields, the only nonzero commutation relations among the basis elements of 𝔤βess\mathfrak{g}^{\rm ess}_{\beta} are the following:

[𝒫t,𝒟β]=(2−β)​𝒫t,[𝒫y,𝒟β]=(3−β)​𝒫y.\displaystyle[\mathcal{P}^{t},\mathcal{D}^{\beta}]=(2-\beta)\mathcal{P}^{t},\hskip 10.00002pt[\mathcal{P}^{y},\mathcal{D}^{\beta}]=(3-\beta)\mathcal{P}^{y}.

The algebra 𝔤βess\mathfrak{g}^{\rm ess}_{\beta} is isomorphic to the algebra A3.4a⊕A1A_{3.4}^{a}\oplus A_{1} with a=(2−β)/(3−β)a=(2-\beta)/(3-\beta), see [46] for notation, which is consistent with Mubarakzyanov’s algebra numeration [37].

8.1 Point symmetry pseudogroup

Theorem 26.

Proof.

The standard algebraic method and its known modifications for computing point symmetry (pseudo)groups of systems of differential equations, see, e.g., [6, 11, 15, 20, 21, 22, 23, 34, 41] and references therein, do not work properly in the case of linear well-determined systems of partial differential equations. This is why we combine the algebraic part of this method with the advanced direct method in an original way. More specifically, Theorem 2 implies that for any fixed β\beta, any point symmetry transformation Φ\Phi of the equation ℱβ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime}_{\beta} is of the form (7a), where U0/U1U^{0}/U^{1} is a solution of ℱβ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime}_{\beta} in view of the last equation in (7c) and the homogeneousness of ℱβ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime}_{\beta} (i.e., C=0C=0 and C~=0\tilde{C}=0). Thus, up to composing with transformations of linear superposition of solutions, we can assume that U0=0U^{0}=0. Then the transformation Φ\Phi preserves the algebra 𝔤βess\mathfrak{g}^{\rm ess}_{\beta} and thus induces an automorphism of this algebra.

Fixing the basis (𝒫t,𝒫y,𝒟β,ℐ)(\mathcal{P}^{t},\mathcal{P}^{y},\mathcal{D}^{\beta},\mathcal{I}), we identify each automorphism of 𝔤βess\mathfrak{g}^{\rm ess}_{\beta} with its matrix in this basis. The automorphisms of the algebra A3.4a⊕A1A_{3.4}^{a}\oplus A_{1}, which is isomorphic to 𝔤βess\mathfrak{g}^{\rm ess}_{\beta}, were first computed in [12, Table 1] in a consistent basis using a different algebra notation (A3.4⊕A1A_{3.4}\oplus A_{1} instead of A3.4−1⊕A1A_{3.4}^{-1}\oplus A_{1} and A3.5α⊕A1A_{3.5}^{\alpha}\oplus A_{1} instead of A3.4α⊕A1A_{3.4}^{\alpha}\oplus A_{1} for −1<α<1-1<\alpha<1); see also [46, Section A.2] for a more convenient exposition. In the case β≠5/2\beta\neq 5/2, the automorphism group Aut⁡(𝔤βess){\rm Aut}(\mathfrak{g}^{\rm ess}_{\beta}) of 𝔤βess\mathfrak{g}^{\rm ess}_{\beta} is constituted by the matrices

(a110a1300a22a230001000a43a44),\displaystyle\begin{pmatrix}a_{11}&0&a_{13}&0\\ 0&a_{22}&a_{23}&0\\ 0&0&1&0\\ 0&0&a_{43}&a_{44}\end{pmatrix}, (29)

where all the involved parameters ai​ja_{ij} are arbitrary real constants with a11​a22​a44≠0a_{11}a_{22}a_{44}\neq 0. If β=5/2\beta=5/2, then the group Aut⁡(𝔤βess){\rm Aut}(\mathfrak{g}^{\rm ess}_{\beta}) is extended, in comparison with the generic case, by the matrices

(0a12a130a210a23000−1000a43a44),\displaystyle\begin{pmatrix}0&a_{12}&a_{13}&0\\ a_{21}&0&a_{23}&0\\ 0&0&-1&0\\ 0&0&a_{43}&a_{44}\end{pmatrix},

where all the involved parameters ai​ja_{ij} are arbitrary real constants with a12​a21​a44≠0a_{12}a_{21}a_{44}\neq 0. The singularity of the value β=5/2\beta=5/2 is related to the fact that the equivalence transformation 𝒥′\mathscr{J}^{\prime} preserves this value of β\beta and, therefore, it induces an additional point symmetry transformation of ℱ5/2′\mathcal{F}^{\prime}_{5/2}. Factoring out the induced transformation from G5/2G_{5/2}, we can consider only automorphisms of the form (29) for each relevant value β\beta.

Pushing forward the basis elements of 𝔤βess\mathfrak{g}^{\rm ess}_{\beta} by Φ\Phi, we obtain the equalities

Φ∗​(𝒫t)=a11​𝒫t,Φ∗​(𝒫y)=a22​𝒫y,Φ∗​(ℐ)=a44​ℐ,\displaystyle\Phi_{*}(\mathcal{P}^{t})=a_{11}\mathcal{P}^{t},\hskip 10.00002pt\Phi_{*}(\mathcal{P}^{y})=a_{22}\mathcal{P}^{y},\hskip 10.00002pt\Phi_{*}(\mathcal{I})=a_{44}\mathcal{I},

In view of this, we can without loss of generality omit the Lie reductions with respect to the subalgebras 𝔰1.4δ\mathfrak{s}_{1.4}^{\delta} and 𝔰2.4κ\mathfrak{s}_{2.4}^{\kappa}. However, this requires us to relax the restriction on the parameter β\beta, from β∈(−∞,5/2]∖{0,2}\beta\in(-\infty,5/2]\setminus\{0,2\} to β∈ℝ∖{0,2,3,5}\beta\in\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0,2,3,5\}. 8.4 Lie reductions of codimensions two and three

The Lie reductions with respect to the subalgebras 𝔰2.1δ\mathfrak{s}_{2.1}^{\delta}, 𝔰2.2ε,0\mathfrak{s}_{2.2}^{\varepsilon,0}, 𝔰2.3κ\mathfrak{s}_{2.3}^{\kappa}, 𝔰2.4κ\mathfrak{s}_{2.4}^{\kappa} and 𝔰3.1κ\mathfrak{s}_{3.1}^{\kappa} do not give new solutions in comparison with the two-step Lie reductions, where the first step is associated with the subalgebra 𝔰1.30\mathfrak{s}_{1.3}^{0} and leads to (1+1)-dimensional linear heat equations with zero or inverse square potentials as reduced equations, and such equations are well studied within the framework of symmetry analysis of differential equations.

This is why the only essential codimension-two Lie reductions of the equations from the class ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime} with β∉{0,2,3,5}\beta\notin\{0,2,3,5\} are those associated with the subalgebras 𝔰2.2ε,κ:=⟨𝒫y+ε​ℐ,𝒫t+κ​ℐ⟩\mathfrak{s}_{2.2}^{\varepsilon,\kappa}:=\langle\mathcal{P}^{y}+\varepsilon\mathcal{I},\mathcal{P}^{t}+\kappa\mathcal{I}\rangle, where ε∈{−1,1}\varepsilon\in\{-1,1\} and κ≠0\kappa\neq 0. A corresponding ansatz is u=eε​y+κ​t​φ​(ω)u=e^{\varepsilon y+\kappa t}\varphi(\omega) with ω=x\omega=x, and the reduced equation for φ\varphi is

|ω|β​φω​ω=(ε​ω+κ)​φ.|\omega|^{\beta}\varphi_{\omega\omega}=(\varepsilon\omega+\kappa)\varphi.

In some particular cases of parameters, we can construct closed-form solutions of this equation.

For example, in the cases β=1\beta=1 and β=4\beta=4, the counterparts of this equation for the corresponding equations of the form (5) coincide with the equations [24, Chapter C, Section 2.273, Eq. (12)] with a=−κa=-\kappa, b2=εb^{2}=\varepsilon, c=1c=1 and a=−εa=-\varepsilon, b2=κb^{2}=\kappa, c=−1c=-1, respectively. At the same time, in view of results of Section 8.3 on 𝔰1.3δ\mathfrak{s}_{1.3}^{\delta}-invariant solutions with δ≠0\delta\neq 0, the consideration of the Lie reduction with respect to the subalgebras 𝔰2.2ε,κ\mathfrak{s}_{2.2}^{\varepsilon,\kappa} makes sense only for β≠1,4\beta\neq 1,4.

For the case β=−1\beta=-1, the change of variable ω~=ω+12​ε​κ\tilde{\omega}=\omega+\frac{1}{2}\varepsilon\kappa results in the equation [24, Chapter C, Section 2.273, Eq. (11)] with a=0a=0, b=−14​ε​κ2b=-\frac{1}{4}\varepsilon\kappa^{2} and c2=−εc^{2}=-\varepsilon, whose general solution is

φ=|ω~|−1/2Re((C1+iC2)Wi​κ216,14(iω~))ifε=1,\displaystyle\varphi=|\tilde{\omega}|^{-1/2}\mathop{\rm Re}\Big((C_{1}+{\rm i}C_{2})W_{\frac{{\rm i}\kappa^{2}}{16},\frac{1}{4}}({\rm i}\tilde{\omega})\Big)\hskip 10.00002pt\mbox{if}\hskip 10.00002pt\varepsilon=1,

8.5 Generating solutions

The simplest way to generate solutions for an equation ℱβ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime}_{\beta} with β∈ℝ∖{0,2,3,5}\beta\in\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0,2,3,5\} is to use its point symmetry pseudogroup from Theorem 26. More specifically, given a solution u=h⁡(t,x,y)u=h(t,x,y) of ℱβ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime}_{\beta}, the action of a transformation of the form (27) leads to the solution

u=σ​h​(|α|β−2​t−λ0,α−1​x,α−1​|α|β−2​y−λ1)+f⁡(t,x,y),\displaystyle u=\sigma h\big(|\alpha|^{\beta-2}t-\lambda_{0},\alpha^{-1}x,\alpha^{-1}|\alpha|^{\beta-2}y-\lambda_{1}\big)+f(t,x,y),

of the same equation. In the case β=5/2\beta=5/2, we can in addition use a transformation of the form (28) and derive the solution

u=σ​h​(sgn(x)​|α|β−2​y−λ0,α​x−1,sgn(x)​α−1​|α|β−2​t−λ1)+f⁡(t,x,y).\displaystyle u=\sigma h\big(\mathop{\rm sgn}\nolimits(x)|\alpha|^{\beta-2}y-\lambda_{0},\alpha x^{-1},\mathop{\rm sgn}\nolimits(x)\alpha^{-1}|\alpha|^{\beta-2}t-\lambda_{1}\big)+f(t,x,y).

Since each equation ℱβ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime}_{\beta} is linear, we can also apply its generalized symmetries to the solution generation following [29]. The differential operators in total derivatives that are associated with the Lie-symmetry vector fields −𝒫t-\mathcal{P}^{t}, −𝒫y-\mathcal{P}^{y}, −𝒟β-\mathcal{D}^{\beta} and ℐ\mathcal{I} are

Pt:=Dt,Py:=Dy,Dβ:=(2−β)​t​Dt+x​Dx+(3−β)​y​Dy\displaystyle\mathrm{P}^{t}:=\mathrm{D}_{t},\hskip 10.00002pt\mathrm{P}^{y}:=\mathrm{D}_{y},\hskip 10.00002pt\mathrm{D}^{\beta}:=(2-\beta)t\mathrm{D}_{t}+x\mathrm{D}_{x}+(3-\beta)y\mathrm{D}_{y}

and the identity operator, respectively. These differential operators generate the associative algebra Υ𝔰\Upsilon_{\mathfrak{s}} associated with the subalgebra 𝔰=⟨𝒫t,𝒫y,𝒟β⟩≃A3.4a\mathfrak{s}=\langle\mathcal{P}^{t},\mathcal{P}^{y},\mathcal{D}^{\beta}\rangle\simeq A_{3.4}^{a} of the algebra 𝔤β\mathfrak{g}_{\beta}, where a:=(β−2)/(β−3)a:=(\beta-2)/(\beta-3). The operators Pt\mathrm{P}^{t} and Dβ\mathrm{D}^{\beta} on the solutions of ℱβ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime}_{\beta} respectively coincide with the operators

P^t:=−x​Dy+|x|β​Dx2andD^β:=(2−β)​t​P^t+x​Dx+(3−β)​y​Dy.\displaystyle\hat{\mathrm{P}}^{t}:=-x\mathrm{D}_{y}+|x|^{\beta}\mathrm{D}_{x}^{2}\hskip 10.00002pt\mbox{and}\hskip 10.00002pt\hat{\mathrm{D}}^{\beta}:=(2-\beta)t\hat{\mathrm{P}}^{t}+x\mathrm{D}_{x}+(3-\beta)y\mathrm{D}_{y}.

Consider the associative algebra Υ¯𝔰\bar{\Upsilon}_{\mathfrak{s}} generated by the operators P^t\hat{\mathrm{P}}^{t}, Py\mathrm{P}^{y} and D^β\hat{\mathrm{D}}^{\beta}. In other words, the algebra Υ¯𝔰\bar{\Upsilon}_{\mathfrak{s}} is subjected to the presentation

Υ¯𝔰=⟨P^t,Py,D^β∣[P^t,D^β]=(2−β)P^t,[Py,D^β]=(3−β)Py,[P^t,Py]=0⟩.\displaystyle\bar{\Upsilon}_{\mathfrak{s}}=\big\langle\hat{\mathrm{P}}^{t},\mathrm{P}^{y},\hat{\mathrm{D}}^{\beta}\mid[\hat{\mathrm{P}}^{t},\hat{\mathrm{D}}^{\beta}]=(2-\beta)\hat{\mathrm{P}}^{t},\,[\mathrm{P}^{y},\hat{\mathrm{D}}^{\beta}]=(3-\beta)\mathrm{P}^{y},\,[\hat{\mathrm{P}}^{t},\mathrm{P}^{y}]=0\big\rangle. (40)
Lemma 32.

The monomials 𝐐α:=(Q1)α1​(Q2)α2​(Q3)α3\mathbf{Q}^{\alpha}:=(\mathrm{Q}^{1})^{\alpha_{1}}(\mathrm{Q}^{2})^{\alpha_{2}}(\mathrm{Q}^{3})^{\alpha_{3}}, where α=(α1,α2,α3)∈ℕ0  3\alpha=(\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2},\alpha_{3})\in\mathbb{N}_{0}^{\,\,3} and (Q1,Q2,Q3)(\mathrm{Q}^{1},\mathrm{Q}^{2},\mathrm{Q}^{3}) is any fixed ordering of P^t\hat{\mathrm{P}}^{t}, Py\mathrm{P}^{y} and D^β\hat{\mathrm{D}}^{\beta}, constitute a basis of the algebra Υ¯𝔰\bar{\Upsilon}_{\mathfrak{s}}.

Proof.

We again make use of Bergman’s diamond lemma [3]. Without loss of generality, we fix the ordering D^β<Py<P^t\hat{\mathrm{D}}^{\beta}<\mathrm{P}^{y}<\hat{\mathrm{P}}^{t} and extend it to the degree lexicographic order on the words in the alphabet (D^β,Py,P^t)(\hat{\mathrm{D}}^{\beta},\mathrm{P}^{y},\hat{\mathrm{P}}^{t}). According to the chosen ordering, the relations in the presentation (40) of the algebra Υ¯𝔰\bar{\Upsilon}_{\mathfrak{s}} can be written as the following reduction system:

P^t​D^β=D^β​P^t+(2−β)​P^t,Py​D^β=D^β​Py+(3−β)​Py,P^t​Py=Py​P^t.\displaystyle\hat{\mathrm{P}}^{t}\hat{\mathrm{D}}^{\beta}=\hat{\mathrm{D}}^{\beta}\hat{\mathrm{P}}^{t}+(2-\beta)\hat{\mathrm{P}}^{t},\hskip 10.00002pt\mathrm{P}^{y}\hat{\mathrm{D}}^{\beta}=\hat{\mathrm{D}}^{\beta}\mathrm{P}^{y}+(3-\beta)\mathrm{P}^{y},\hskip 10.00002pt\hat{\mathrm{P}}^{t}\mathrm{P}^{y}=\mathrm{P}^{y}\hat{\mathrm{P}}^{t}.

It has exactly one overlap ambiguity, P^t​Py​D^β\hat{\mathrm{P}}^{t}\mathrm{P}^{y}\hat{\mathrm{D}}^{\beta}, which is resolvable since

P^t​Py​D^β=Py​P^t​D^β=Py​D^β​P^t+(2−β)​Py​P^t=D^β​Py​P^t+(3−β)​Py​P^t+(2−β)​Py​P^t,P^t​Py​D^β=P^t​D^β​Py+(3−β)​P^t​Py=D^β​P^t​Py+(2−β)​P^t​Py+(3−β)​P^t​Py=D^β​Py​P^t+(2−β)​Py​P^t+(3−β)​Py​P^t.\displaystyle\begin{split}\hat{\mathrm{P}}^{t}\mathrm{P}^{y}\hat{\mathrm{D}}^{\beta}&{}=\mathrm{P}^{y}\hat{\mathrm{P}}^{t}\hat{\mathrm{D}}^{\beta}=\mathrm{P}^{y}\hat{\mathrm{D}}^{\beta}\hat{\mathrm{P}}^{t}+(2-\beta)\mathrm{P}^{y}\hat{\mathrm{P}}^{t}=\hat{\mathrm{D}}^{\beta}\mathrm{P}^{y}\hat{\mathrm{P}}^{t}+(3-\beta)\mathrm{P}^{y}\hat{\mathrm{P}}^{t}+(2-\beta)\mathrm{P}^{y}\hat{\mathrm{P}}^{t},\\[4.30554pt] \hat{\mathrm{P}}^{t}\mathrm{P}^{y}\hat{\mathrm{D}}^{\beta}&{}=\hat{\mathrm{P}}^{t}\hat{\mathrm{D}}^{\beta}\mathrm{P}^{y}+(3-\beta)\hat{\mathrm{P}}^{t}\mathrm{P}^{y}=\hat{\mathrm{D}}^{\beta}\hat{\mathrm{P}}^{t}\mathrm{P}^{y}+(2-\beta)\hat{\mathrm{P}}^{t}\mathrm{P}^{y}+(3-\beta)\hat{\mathrm{P}}^{t}\mathrm{P}^{y}\\ &{}=\hat{\mathrm{D}}^{\beta}\mathrm{P}^{y}\hat{\mathrm{P}}^{t}+(2-\beta)\mathrm{P}^{y}\hat{\mathrm{P}}^{t}+(3-\beta)\mathrm{P}^{y}\hat{\mathrm{P}}^{t}.\end{split}

Thus, the diamond lemma implies that the monomials of the form (P^t)α1​(Py)α2​(D^β)α3(\hat{\mathrm{P}}^{t})^{\alpha_{1}}(\mathrm{P}^{y})^{\alpha_{2}}(\hat{\mathrm{D}}^{\beta})^{\alpha_{3}} constitute an ℝ\mathbb{R}-basis of the algebra Υ¯𝔰\bar{\Upsilon}_{\mathfrak{s}}. Similar arguments work for all the other orderings of P^t\hat{\mathrm{P}}^{t}, Py\mathrm{P}^{y} and D^β\hat{\mathrm{D}}^{\beta}. ∎

Corollary 33.

The algebra Υ¯𝔰\bar{\Upsilon}_{\mathfrak{s}} is isomorphic to the universal enveloping algebra 𝔘⁡(A3.4a)\mathfrak{U}(A_{3.4}^{a}) of the Lie algebra A3.4a=⟨e1,e2,e3⟩A_{3.4}^{a}=\langle e_{1},e_{2},e_{3}\rangle, [e1,e3]=e1[e_{1},e_{3}]=e_{1}, [e2,e3]=a​e2[e_{2},e_{3}]=ae_{2}, where a=(2−β)/(3−β)a=(2-\beta)/(3-\beta).

Proof.

The correspondence −𝒫t↦P^t-\mathcal{P}^{t}\mapsto\hat{\mathrm{P}}^{t}, −𝒫y↦Py-\mathcal{P}^{y}\mapsto\mathrm{P}^{y} and −𝒟β↦D^β-\mathcal{D}^{\beta}\mapsto\hat{\mathrm{D}}^{\beta} by linearity extends to the Lie algebra homomorphism φ\varphi from 𝔰=⟨𝒫t,𝒫y,𝒟β⟩\mathfrak{s}=\langle\mathcal{P}^{t},\mathcal{P}^{y},\mathcal{D}^{\beta}\rangle to the Lie algebra Υ¯𝔰(−)\bar{\Upsilon}_{\mathfrak{s}}^{(-)} associated with the associative algebra Υ¯𝔰\bar{\Upsilon}_{\mathfrak{s}}, φ:𝔰→Υ¯𝔰(−)\varphi\colon\mathfrak{s}\to\smash{\bar{\Upsilon}_{\mathfrak{s}}^{(-)}}. By the universal property of the universal enveloping algebra 𝔘⁡(𝔰)\mathfrak{U}(\mathfrak{s}), the Lie algebra homomorphism φ\varphi extends to the (unital) associative algebra homomorphism φ^:𝔘⁡(𝔰)→Υ¯𝔰\hat{\varphi}\colon\mathfrak{U}(\mathfrak{s})\to\bar{\Upsilon}_{\mathfrak{s}}, i.e., φ=φ^∘ι\varphi=\hat{\varphi}\circ\iota as homomorphisms of vector spaces, where ι:𝔰→𝔘⁡(𝔰)\iota\colon\mathfrak{s}\to\mathfrak{U}(\mathfrak{s}) is the canonical embedding of 𝔰\mathfrak{s} in 𝔘⁡(𝔰)\mathfrak{U}(\mathfrak{s}). Since the algebra Υ𝔰\Upsilon_{\mathfrak{s}} is generated by φ⁡(𝔰)\varphi(\mathfrak{s}), the homomorphism φ^\hat{\varphi} is surjective. Fixed an ordering of the basis elements of 𝔰\mathfrak{s}, in view of the Poincaré–Birkhoff–Witt theorem, the homomorphism φ^\hat{\varphi} maps the corresponding Poincaré–Birkhoff–Witt basis of 𝔘⁡(𝔰)\mathfrak{U}(\mathfrak{s}) to a basis of Υ¯𝔰\bar{\Upsilon}_{\mathfrak{s}}. Therefore, φ^\hat{\varphi} is an isomorphism. The isomorphism 𝔰≃A3.4a\mathfrak{s}\simeq A_{3.4}^{a} implies the isomorphism 𝔘⁡(𝔰)≃𝔘⁡(A3.4a)\mathfrak{U}(\mathfrak{s})\simeq\mathfrak{U}(A_{3.4}^{a}). ∎

Corollary 34.

The algebra Υ¯𝔰\bar{\Upsilon}_{\mathfrak{s}} is isomorphic to the algebra ⟨(𝐐αu)∂u∣α∈ℕ0  3⟩\big\langle(\mathbf{Q}^{\alpha}u)\partial_{u}\mid\alpha\in\mathbb{N}_{0}^{\,\,3}\big\rangle of canonical representatives for a subalgebra of the quotient algebra of generalized symmetries of an equation ℱβ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime}_{\beta} with β∈ℝ∖{0,2,3,5}\beta\in\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0,2,3,5\} with respect to the equivalence of generalized symmetries.

Similarly to what has been indicated in Sections 6 and 7, we use elements of the algebra Υ¯𝔰\bar{\Upsilon}_{\mathfrak{s}} to generate solutions of the equation ℱβ′\mathcal{F}_{\beta}^{\prime}. More specifically, acting on a solution u=h⁡(t,x,y)u=h(t,x,y) of this equation by an arbitrary element

Q=∑(α1,α2,α3)∈ℕ0  3cα1​α2​α3​(Q1)α1​(Q2)α2​(Q3)α3Q=\sum_{(\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2},\alpha_{3})\in\mathbb{N}_{0}^{\,\,3}}c_{\alpha_{1}\alpha_{2}\alpha_{3}}(\mathrm{Q}^{1})^{\alpha_{1}}(\mathrm{Q}^{2})^{\alpha_{2}}(\mathrm{Q}^{3})^{\alpha_{3}}

of the algebra Υ¯𝔰\bar{\Upsilon}_{\mathfrak{s}}, gives the solution Q​hQh of the same equation. Here all but finitely many (real) constants cα1​α2​α3c_{\alpha_{1}\alpha_{2}\alpha_{3}} are equal to zero, and any ordering in {D^β,Py,P^t}\{\hat{\mathrm{D}}^{\beta},\mathrm{P}^{y},\hat{\mathrm{P}}^{t}\} can be fixed. In view of Corollary 34, the latter generation is consistent with the generation of solutions using generalized symmetries as indicated in [29, Section 6], however, since the algebra of generalized symmetries of ℱβ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime}_{\beta} is yet not described, we use its known subalgebra.

Nevertheless, depending on hh and cα1​α2​α3c_{\alpha_{1}\alpha_{2}\alpha_{3}}, this formula can result in a known or even the zero solution. We analyze which solutions generated according to this from Lie invariant solutions of ℱβ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime}_{\beta} may be of interest. It suffices to consider only the solutions that are invariant with respect to the subalgebras 𝔰1.1κ=⟨𝒟β+κ​ℐ⟩\mathfrak{s}_{1.1}^{\kappa}=\langle\mathcal{D}^{\beta}+\kappa\mathcal{I}\rangle, 𝔰1.2ε,κ=⟨𝒫y+ε​𝒫t+κ​ℐ⟩\mathfrak{s}_{1.2}^{\varepsilon,\kappa}=\langle\mathcal{P}^{y}+\varepsilon\mathcal{P}^{t}+\kappa\mathcal{I}\rangle, 𝔰1.3δ=⟨𝒫y+δ​ℐ⟩\mathfrak{s}_{1.3}^{\delta}=\langle\mathcal{P}^{y}+\delta\mathcal{I}\rangle, 𝔰2.2ε,κ=⟨𝒫y+ε​ℐ,𝒫t+κ​ℐ⟩\mathfrak{s}_{2.2}^{\varepsilon,\kappa}=\langle\mathcal{P}^{y}+\varepsilon\mathcal{I},\mathcal{P}^{t}+\kappa\mathcal{I}\rangle, with ε=±1\varepsilon=\pm 1, δ∈{−1,0,1}\delta\in\{-1,0,1\}, κ∈ℝ\kappa\in\mathbb{R} and, for the last subalgebra family, κ≠0\kappa\neq 0, see Section 8.2. These solutions were discussed in Sections 8.3 and 8.4. In view of the structure of the algebra 𝔤β\mathfrak{g}_{\beta} with β∈ℝ∖{0,2,3,5}\beta\in\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0,2,3,5\}, the analysis reduces to that for single monomials (D^β)α1​(Py)α2​(P^t)α3(\hat{\mathrm{D}}^{\beta})^{\alpha_{1}}(\mathrm{P}^{y})^{\alpha_{2}}(\hat{\mathrm{P}}^{t})^{\alpha_{3}}.

1.1. The vector field 𝒟β+κ​ℐ\mathcal{D}^{\beta}+\kappa\mathcal{I} corresponds to the differential operator D^β−κ\hat{\mathrm{D}}^{\beta}-\kappa. Since P^t​D^β=(D^β+2−β)​P^t\hat{\mathrm{P}}^{t}\hat{\mathrm{D}}^{\beta}=(\hat{\mathrm{D}}^{\beta}+2-\beta)\hat{\mathrm{P}}^{t} and Py​D^β=(D^β+3−β)​Py\mathrm{P}^{y}\hat{\mathrm{D}}^{\beta}=(\hat{\mathrm{D}}^{\beta}+3-\beta)\mathrm{P}^{y}, we have
