9 Conclusion

The class of ultraparabolic (1+2)-dimensional Kolmogorov backward equations with power diffusivity ℱ\mathcal{F} and its properly gauged counterpart ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime} have many outstanding properties from the perspective of symmetry analysis of differential equations. As expected, the generic elements of the class ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime} are related to one of the inequivalent cases of Lie symmetry extension within the superclass ℱ¯\bar{\mathcal{F}} of the ultraparabolic linear (1+2)-dimensional second-order partial differential equations, which is a subcase of a case with at least four-dimensional decomposable solvable essential Lie invariance algebras. Moreover, specific exponents 0, 2, 3 and 5 of power diffusivity correspond to additional Lie symmetry extensions.

At the same time, the number of surprising properties of the classes ℱ\mathcal{F} and ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime} is essentially greater than those we expected.

The class ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime} admits the nontrivial discrete equivalence transformation (4), which is the only essential among elements of the equivalence group Gℱ′∼G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}^{\prime}} in the course of group classification of this class. Under passing to the class ℱ\mathcal{F}, this transformation induces elements from the complement of the action groupoid of the group Gℱ∼G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}} in the groupoid 𝒢ℱ∼\mathcal{G}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}}, and thus it is associated with no element of Gℱ∼G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}}. This shows the naturality and, moreover, the necessity of the gauge α=0\alpha=0.

There are only two Gℱ′∼G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}^{\prime}}-inequivalent cases of essential Lie symmetry extensions within the class ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime}. They are associated with the remarkable Fokker–Planck equation ℱ0′\mathcal{F}^{\prime}_{0} and the fine Kolmogorov backward equation ℱ2′\mathcal{F}^{\prime}_{2}. Furthermore, these are equations that are singular with respect to their symmetry properties in the entire superclass ℱ¯\bar{\mathcal{F}}, representing the cases with maximum eight-dimensional and nonsolvable five-dimensional essential Lie symmetry extensions, respectively. As a result, the study of ℱ0′\mathcal{F}^{\prime}_{0} and ℱ2′\mathcal{F}^{\prime}_{2} in [27, 29, 44] provides a significant part of symmetry analysis of elements of not only the classes ℱ\mathcal{F} and ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime} but also their superclass ℱ¯\bar{\mathcal{F}}.

The equations ℱ0′\mathcal{F}^{\prime}_{0} and ℱ2′\mathcal{F}^{\prime}_{2} are also distinguished by other symmetry properties. They admit a number of nontrivial hidden Lie symmetries that are associated with their codimension-one Lie reductions to the (1+1)-dimensional linear heat equations with inverse square or zero potentials. Moreover, all the closed-form Lie invariant solutions that can be constructed for ℱ0′\mathcal{F}^{\prime}_{0} and ℱ2′\mathcal{F}^{\prime}_{2} are related to such reductions. These solutions constitute wide families and, furthermore, can be used as seeds for generating new solutions via acting by recursion operators related to Lie symmetries, and such generation indeed efficiently works for ℱ0′\mathcal{F}^{\prime}_{0} and ℱ2′\mathcal{F}^{\prime}_{2}.

Even more surprising is that, among the other equations in the class ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime} up to the Gℱ′∼G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}^{\prime}}-equivalence, only the equation ℱ1′\mathcal{F}^{\prime}_{1} possesses all the above properties of ℱ0′\mathcal{F}^{\prime}_{0} and ℱ2′\mathcal{F}^{\prime}_{2}, except the extension of essential Lie invariance algebras. This is why the singularity of ℱ1′\mathcal{F}^{\prime}_{1} within the class ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime} can be found out only after the comprehensive study of Lie reductions of the equations from this class.

Another but less singular equation is ℱ−1′\mathcal{F}^{\prime}_{-1}. Its singularity becomes apparent only in the course of carrying out its codimension-two Lie reductions to ordinary differential equations that integrate, in contrast to their analogues for regular elements of the class ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime}, in terms of Whittaker functions. The solutions of ℱ−1′\mathcal{F}^{\prime}_{-1} constructed in this way can also be used as seeds for generating new solutions via acting by a recursion operator arising from a Lie symmetry.

We have found hidden Lie symmetries for the generic equations from the class ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime}, but their number is essentially less than for the singular equations from these class with β∈{0,1,2,3,4,5}\beta\in\{0,1,2,3,4,5\}. All of these symmetries are associated with codimension-one Lie reductions.

In total, we have singled out eight values of the arbitrary element β\beta, including Gℱ′∼G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}^{\prime}}-equivalent counterparts, −1-1, 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6. An open question is whether there exist other properties that distinguish the listed values. It is also not clear whether the study of more complicated structures like generalized symmetries or reduction modules can allow one to reveal the singularity of some values of β\beta that are regular from the point of view of Lie and hidden Lie symmetries, the construction of families of Lie-invariant solutions and their extension by recursion operators.

The results of the present paper has several novel features.

We not only have completely solved the properly posed group classification problems for the classes ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime} and ℱ\mathcal{F} with respect to equivalences of two kinds but have also computed the point symmetry pseudogroups of all equations from these classes. The point symmetry pseudogroups of the equations ℱβ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime}_{\beta} with β=0\beta=0, β=5\beta=5, β=2\beta=2, β=3\beta=3 and β∈ℝ∖{0,2,3,5}\beta\in\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0,2,3,5\} are given in Theorems 18, 21, 23, 25 and 26, respectively, which provides the exhaustive descriptions of the fundamental groupoids 𝒢ℱ′f\mathcal{G}^{\rm f}_{\mathcal{F}^{\prime}} and, hence, 𝒢ℱf\mathcal{G}^{\rm f}_{\mathcal{F}}. Combining the above result on 𝒢ℱ′f\mathcal{G}^{\rm f}_{\mathcal{F}^{\prime}} with Theorem 4(iv), we obtain the complete description of the entire equivalence groupoid 𝒢ℱ′∼\mathcal{G}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}^{\prime}}.

Theorem 35.

The class ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime} is semi-normalized. Its equivalence groupoid 𝒢ℱ′∼\mathcal{G}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}^{\prime}} is the Frobenius product of the action groupoid of the subgroup generated by the discrete equivalence transformation 𝒥′\mathscr{J}^{\prime} and the fundamental groupoid 𝒢ℱ′f={(β,Φ,β)∣Φ∈Gβ,β∈ℝ}\mathcal{G}^{\rm f}_{\mathcal{F}^{\prime}}=\{(\beta,\Phi,\beta)\mid\Phi\in G_{\beta},\,\beta\in\mathbb{R}\}, where GβG_{\beta} is the point-symmetry (pseudo)group of the equation ℱβ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime}_{\beta}, presented in Theorems 18, 21, 23, 25 and 26 for β=0\beta=0, β=5\beta=5, β=2\beta=2, β=3\beta=3 and β∈ℝ∖{0,2,3,5}\beta\in\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0,2,3,5\}, respectively.

Corollary 5 combined with Theorem 35 completes the description of 𝒢ℱ∼\mathcal{G}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}}.

Theorem 36.

The equivalence groupoid 𝒢ℱ∼\mathcal{G}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}} is constituted by the admissible transformations

((α,β),π∗​𝒮​(α~)∘Φ∘π∗​𝒮​(−α),(α~,β~)),\displaystyle\big((\alpha,\beta),\pi_{*}\mathscr{S}(\tilde{\alpha})\circ\Phi\circ\pi_{*}\mathscr{S}(-\alpha),(\tilde{\alpha},\tilde{\beta})\big),

where (β,Φ,β~)∈𝒢ℱ′∼(\beta,\Phi,\tilde{\beta})\in\mathcal{G}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}^{\prime}}.

We have first applied Hydon’s automorphism-based version of the algebraic method [20, 21, 22, 23] to compute equivalence groups of classes of differential equations, which are the groups Gℱ∼G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}} and Gℱ′∼G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}^{\prime}}. At the same time, the required automorphism groups of the associated equivalence algebras 𝔤ℱ∼\mathfrak{g}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}} and 𝔤ℱ′∼\mathfrak{g}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}^{\prime}} cannot be found in the straightforward “brute-force” way. This is why we needed first to construct a sufficient number of megaideals of these algebras and then to take into account the derived constraints on entries of the automorphism matrices in the course of the regular computation of the automorphism groups. It was unexpected that the megaideals preliminarily constructed using their basic properties exhaust the entire sets of megaideals of the corresponding algebras.

The groups Gℱ∼G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}} and Gℱ′∼G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}^{\prime}} have also been constructed using the original advanced version of the direct method. There are two outputs of the double computation. It provides a cross-check of the correctness of the obtained groups, which is important since knowing them underlies all aspects of symmetry analysis of equations from the classes ℱ\mathcal{F} and ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime}. Due to the double computation, we can also compare the effectiveness of the applied method. We did not expect that the advanced version of the direct method turns out to be more efficient than the algebraic method.

In general, the study of the particular equivalence groupoids and equivalence groups in the present paper gives a justified insight into further development of computational tools for such studies.

To find the point symmetry pseudogroup GβG_{\beta} of a generic equation ℱβ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime}_{\beta} in the class ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime}, we have used an original combination of the above methods, see the proof of Theorem 26. We have first applied the advanced version of the direct method to prove the factorization of the pseudogroup GβG_{\beta} and the maximal Lie invariance algebra 𝔤β\mathfrak{g}_{\beta} of ℱβ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime}_{\beta} into their essential parts and those associated with the linear superposition of solutions. The later parts are known and can be neglected. The fact that the adjoint action of the group GβessG^{\rm ess}_{\beta} preserves the algebra 𝔤βess\mathfrak{g}^{\rm ess}_{\beta} has allowed us to use techniques of Hydon’s algebraic method for obtaining a restrictive form for elements of the group GβessG^{\rm ess}_{\beta}, which is parameterized by six constants. Then we complete the computation of this group by the direct method, deriving two constraints for these parameters.

The classes ℱ\mathcal{F} and ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime} are constituted by linear differential equations. This is why it was natural and instructive to generate new wide solution families of equations from these classes by acting with recursion operators associated with their essential Lie symmetries. We have singled out, up to the Gℱ∼G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}}- and Gℱ′∼G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}^{\prime}}-equivalences within the respective classes and up to the GβG_{\beta}-equivalence for each particular value of β\beta, all nontrivial generations among the above ones and then carried out them. This provided the first example in the literature on exhaustive study of such generations for a class of linear differential equations. The first similar examples for single differential linear equations were presented in [29] and [44] for the fine Kolmogorov backward equation ℱ2′\mathcal{F}^{\prime}_{2} and the remarkable Fokker–Planck equation ℱ0′\mathcal{F}^{\prime}_{0}, respectively.

Despite the diverse results obtained for the classes ℱ\mathcal{F} and ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime} and their particular elements in [27, 29, 44] and in the present paper, there are still many open problems on these objects, not to mention the superclass ℱ¯\bar{\mathcal{F}}.

We have comprehensively studied the generation of solutions of equations from ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime} by their recursion operators that are related to their Lie symmetries. General linear recursion operators, which are associated with linear genuinely generalized symmetries, are also relevant for such generation but their classification is much more complicated than the classification of recursion operators stemming from Lie symmetries. We proved in [44] that the entire algebra of generalized symmetries of the remarkable Fokker–Planck equation ℱ0′\mathcal{F}^{\prime}_{0} is generated with successively acting by its Lie-symmetry operators on the trivial Lie symmetry u∂uu\partial_{u}. We also reasonably conjecture the analogous claim for the fine Kolmogorov backward equation ℱ2′\mathcal{F}^{\prime}_{2} in [29, Section 6]. At the same time, we have no conjecture on generalized symmetries of equations ℱβ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime}_{\beta} with β∈ℝ∖{0,2,3,5}\beta\in\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0,2,3,5\}.

In the context of the theory of singular reduction modules [10] and in view of the ultraparabolicity of equations from the classes ℱ\mathcal{F} and ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime}, it will be instructive to study reduction modules of these equations. In comparison with Lie symmetries, the main obstacle of finding non-Lie reduction modules is that it reduces to solving nonlinear determining equations even for linear differential equations, which makes the related computations highly nontrivial and cumbersome. For example, even for the simplest class constituted by linear second-order partial differential equations with two independent variables, an analogous study was carried out only for the subclass of evolution equations [45].

Local conservation laws of equations from the class ℱ\mathcal{F} were described in [56], which can be viewed as a preliminary step for the further consideration of nonlocal structures associated with these equations, e.g., potential conservation laws and potential symmetries. With this objective in mind, one should remember the principal difference between the two- and multi-dimensional cases in this aspect [1, Theorem 2.7]. More specifically, for the existence of nontrivial potential structures in the latter case, one should gauge potentials arising from the conservation laws, and the selection of suitable and natural gauges can be still carried out only in a heuristic way.

All the above problems can be extended to equations from the superclass ℱ¯\bar{\mathcal{F}}. This class has been extensively studied for the past couple of decades. Its partial preliminary group classification was carried out in [13]. Some subclasses of ℱ¯\bar{\mathcal{F}} were considered within the Lie-symmetry framework in [18, 31, 53, 51, 52, 56]. Despite the number of papers on this subject, there are still many open problems in the symmetry analysis of the entire class ℱ¯\bar{\mathcal{F}}, its subclasses and even particular equations from this class, as can be seen from the above discussion on the classes ℱ\mathcal{F} and ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime} and on the equations ℱ0′\mathcal{F}^{\prime}_{0} and ℱ2′\mathcal{F}^{\prime}_{2}. We are close to completely solve the group classification problem for the class ℱ¯\bar{\mathcal{F}} using the algebraic approach, and this involves almost all recently developed advanced techniques of group classification and the famous description of finite-dimensional Lie algebras of vector fields on the real plane, see [33, pp. 122–178] for the first presentation and [16] for the modern and enhanced version of this result.

Appendix A Algebraic method for computing equivalence groups

The straightforward construction of the equivalence group of a class of differential equations by the direct method in general leads to cumbersome and complicated computations. We simplify finding the equivalence groups Gℱ∼G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}} and Gℱ′∼G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}^{\prime}} due to using an advanced version of the direct method and knowing the equivalence groupoid of the superclass ℱ¯\bar{\mathcal{F}}, which is described in Theorem 2. Nevertheless, it is still instructive to find the groups Gℱ∼G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}} and Gℱ′∼G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}^{\prime}} by Hydon’s algebraic method [20, 21, 22, 23] extended to equivalence groups in [5], which in addition leads to the double-check of Theorems 6 and 10. The algebraic method is based on knowing the corresponding equivalence algebra, which should be computed independently using the infinitesimal approach. In the course of this computation, we can assume that the constant arbitrary elements α\alpha and β\beta of the class ℱ\mathcal{F} (resp. β\beta of the class ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime}) play the role of additional dependent variables satisfying the equations αt=αx=αy=0\alpha_{t}=\alpha_{x}=\alpha_{y}=0 and βt=βx=βy=0\beta_{t}=\beta_{x}=\beta_{y}=0 (resp. βt=βx=βy=0\beta_{t}=\beta_{x}=\beta_{y}=0). The corresponding infinitesimal invariance condition should be split with respect to both the parametric jet variables and the arbitrary elements α\alpha and β\beta (resp. the arbitrary element β\beta). Since the equivalence algebras 𝔤ℱ∼\mathfrak{g}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}} and 𝔤ℱ′∼\mathfrak{g}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}^{\prime}} are finite-dimensional, we proceed with the original automorphism-based version of the algebraic method by Hydon [20, 21, 22, 23]. In fact, this is the first example of such a computation in the literature, see [5, Section 4] for the first application of the megaideal-based version of the same method to finding the equivalence group of a class of differential equations.

A.1 The original class

Despite the fact that the dimension of the algebra 𝔤:=𝔤ℱ∼\mathfrak{g}:=\mathfrak{g}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}} is not high, see Corollary 8, the direct construction of the automorphism group Aut⁡(𝔤){\rm Aut}(\mathfrak{g}) using symbolic computation programs seems expensive, if at all possible. To make the construction feasible, we first find a sufficient number of megaideals [46] of 𝔤\mathfrak{g}, i.e., linear subspaces of 𝔤\mathfrak{g} that are stable with respect to the action of Aut⁡(𝔤){\rm Aut}(\mathfrak{g}); another name for megaideals is fully characteristic ideals [19, Exercise 14.1.1]. The choice of a basis of 𝔤\mathfrak{g} agreed with the megaideal hierarchy 𝔤\mathfrak{g} guarantees the presence of an essential number of zero entries in the matrix of a general automorphism of 𝔤\mathfrak{g}. The more megaideals we construct, the simpler computations become.

In view of elementary properties of megaideals, all elements of the derived series, the upper and the lower central series of 𝔤\mathfrak{g}, including the center 𝔷⁡(𝔤)\mathfrak{z}(\mathfrak{g}) and the derivative 𝔤′\mathfrak{g}^{\prime} of 𝔤\mathfrak{g}, are megaideals of 𝔤\mathfrak{g}. Thus,

𝔪1:=𝔤′′=⟨∂u⟩,𝔪2:=𝔷(𝔤′)=⟨∂u,x∂u⟩,𝔪4:=𝔤ℱ3=[𝔤,𝔤ℱ′]=⟨∂u,x∂u,(tx−y)∂u⟩\displaystyle\mathfrak{m}_{1}:=\mathfrak{g}^{\prime\prime}=\langle\partial_{u}\rangle,\ \ \mathfrak{m}_{2}:=\mathfrak{z}(\mathfrak{g}^{\prime})=\langle\partial_{u},x\partial_{u}\rangle,\ \ \mathfrak{m}_{4}:=\mathfrak{g}^{3}_{\mathcal{F}}=[\mathfrak{g},\mathfrak{g}^{\prime}_{\mathcal{F}}]=\langle\partial_{u},x\partial_{u},(tx-y)\partial_{u}\rangle

are megaideals of 𝔤\mathfrak{g}. A useful tool for constructing megaideals of Lie algebras is [15, Proposition 1], which states that if 𝔦0\mathfrak{i}_{0}, 𝔦1\mathfrak{i}_{1} and 𝔦2\mathfrak{i}_{2} are the megaideals of 𝔤\mathfrak{g}, then the set 𝔰\mathfrak{s} of elements from 𝔦0\mathfrak{i}_{0} whose commutators with arbitrary elements from 𝔦1\mathfrak{i}_{1} belong to 𝔦2\mathfrak{i}_{2} is also a megaideal of 𝔤\mathfrak{g}. By considering (𝔦0,𝔦1,𝔦2)=(𝔤,𝔤,𝔪1)(\mathfrak{i}_{0},\mathfrak{i}_{1},\mathfrak{i}_{2})=(\mathfrak{g},\mathfrak{g},\mathfrak{m}_{1}) and (𝔦0,𝔦1,𝔦2)=(𝔤,𝔤,𝔪3)(\mathfrak{i}_{0},\mathfrak{i}_{1},\mathfrak{i}_{2})=(\mathfrak{g},\mathfrak{g},\mathfrak{m}_{3}) we respectively obtain the megaideals

𝔪3:=⟨∂u,∂y⟩,𝔪5:=⟨∂u,∂y,∂x+t∂y+∂α⟩.\displaystyle\mathfrak{m}_{3}:=\langle\partial_{u},\partial_{y}\rangle,\hskip 10.00002pt\mathfrak{m}_{5}:=\langle\partial_{u},\partial_{y},\partial_{x}+t\partial_{y}+\partial_{\alpha}\rangle.

The sum of megaideals is a megaideal. Taking (𝔦0,𝔦1,𝔦2)=(𝔪,𝔤,{0})(\mathfrak{i}_{0},\mathfrak{i}_{1},\mathfrak{i}_{2})=(\mathfrak{m},\mathfrak{g},\{0\}), we derive that the centralizer C𝔤​(𝔪)\mathrm{C}_{\mathfrak{g}}(\mathfrak{m}) of a megaideal 𝔪\mathfrak{m} is a megaideal. By this, we obtain the megaideal

𝔪6:=C𝔤(𝔪2+𝔪3)=⟨∂u,x∂u,∂y,∂t⟩.\displaystyle\mathfrak{m}_{6}:=\mathrm{C}_{\mathfrak{g}}(\mathfrak{m}_{2}+\mathfrak{m}_{3})=\langle\partial_{u},x\partial_{u},\partial_{y},\partial_{t}\rangle.

Applying the technique suggested in [11, Lemma 10], we construct one more megaideal in 𝔤\mathfrak{g}.

which should coincide with (2). This results in the equation

|c22​x+c21|β~=Δ2​sgn(c12​x+c11)​|x|β​|c12​x+c11|β~−5.|c_{22}x+c_{21}|^{\tilde{\beta}}=\Delta^{2}\mathop{\rm sgn}\nolimits(c_{12}x+c_{11})|x|^{\beta}|c_{12}x+c_{11}|^{\tilde{\beta}-5}.

Hence sgn(c12​x+c11)=1\mathop{\rm sgn}\nolimits(c_{12}x+c_{11})=1. In view of Lemma 3 and the inequality c11​c22−c21​c12≠0c_{11}c_{22}-c_{21}c_{12}\neq 0, in the case c22=0c_{22}=0, we successively derive c12​c21≠0c_{12}c_{21}\neq 0, c11=0c_{11}=0, c12=sgnxc_{12}=\mathop{\rm sgn}\nolimits x, c21=±sgnxc_{21}=\pm\mathop{\rm sgn}\nolimits x and β=5−β~\beta=5-\tilde{\beta}. Analogously, for c22≠0c_{22}\neq 0 we obtain c12=0c_{12}=0, c11≠0c_{11}\neq 0, c21=0c_{21}=0, c11=1c_{11}=1, β~=β\tilde{\beta}=\beta, |c22|β−2=1|c_{22}|^{\beta-2}=1 and thus c22=±1c_{22}=\pm 1. Hence, there are only three independent discrete equivalence transformations in Gℱ′∼G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}^{\prime}}, ℐu′\mathscr{I}^{\prime}_{u}, ℐs′\mathscr{I}^{\prime}_{\rm s} and 𝒥′\mathscr{J}^{\prime}, which are respectively associated with the values ε=−1\varepsilon=-1, (ε,c22)=(−1,1)(\varepsilon,c_{22})=(-1,1) (if the other parameters in these two cases take the values as for the identity transformation) and (c11,c12,c21,c22,ε)=(0,sgnx,sgnx,0,−sgnx)(c_{11},c_{12},c_{21},c_{22},\varepsilon)=(0,\mathop{\rm sgn}\nolimits x,\mathop{\rm sgn}\nolimits x,0,-\mathop{\rm sgn}\nolimits x), see Corollary 14.

Appendix B Darboux transformations
of linear heat equations with potentials

Consider a (1+1)-dimensional linear heat equations with an arbitrary potential V=V⁡(t,x)V=V(t,x),

ut−ux​x+V⁡(t,x)​u=0.\displaystyle u_{t}-u_{xx}+V(t,x)u=0. (41)

By W⁡(f1,…,fk)\mathrm{W}(f^{1},\dots,f^{k}) we denote the Wronskian of sufficiently smooth functions f1f^{1}, …, fkf^{k} of (t,x)(t,x) with respect to xx, W⁡(f1,…,fk)=det(∂xl′−1fl)l,l′=1,…,k\mathrm{W}(f^{1},\dots,f^{k})=\det(\partial_{x}^{l^{\prime}-1}f^{l})_{l,l^{\prime}=1,\dots,k}. The Darboux transformation

u~=DT⁡[f1,…,fk]​u:=W⁡(f1,…,fk,u)W⁡(f1,…,fk),\tilde{u}=\mathrm{DT}[f^{1},\dots,f^{k}]u:=\frac{\mathrm{W}(f^{1},\dots,f^{k},u)}{\mathrm{W}(f^{1},\dots,f^{k})},

with a fixed tuple (f1,…,fk)(f^{1},\dots,f^{k}) of solutions of (41) maps the solution set of (41) onto the solution set of the equation u~t−u~x​x+V~​(t,x)​u~=0\tilde{u}_{t}-\tilde{u}_{xx}+\tilde{V}(t,x)\tilde{u}=0, where

V~=V−2​((W⁡(f1,…,fk))xW⁡(f1,…,fk))x,\tilde{V}=V-2\left(\frac{\big(\mathrm{W}(f^{1},\dots,f^{k})\big)_{x}}{\mathrm{W}(f^{1},\dots,f^{k})}\right)_{x},

see [35, 48]. An evident relation is established by Darboux transformations between (1+1)-dimensional linear heat equations with inverse square potentials, V=−μ​x−2V=-\mu x^{-2}, where μ\mu is an arbitrary constant with μ⩽14\mu\leqslant\frac{1}{4}. The function u=|x|αu=|x|^{\alpha} with α=12±(14−μ)1/2\alpha=\frac{1}{2}\pm(\frac{1}{4}-\mu)^{1/2} is a solution of the equation

ut=ux​x+μ​x−2​u,\displaystyle u_{t}=u_{xx}+\mu x^{-2}u, (42)

and the corresponding Darboux transformation DT⁡[|x|α]\mathrm{DT}[|x|^{\alpha}] maps this equation to the equation u~t=u~x​x+μ~​x−2​u~\tilde{u}_{t}=\tilde{u}_{xx}+\tilde{\mu}x^{-2}\tilde{u} with μ~=μ−2​α\tilde{\mu}=\mu-2\alpha.

The most interesting is the case when solutions of (1+1)-dimensional linear heat equations with inverse square potentials are expressed in terms of the general solution of the (1+1)-dimensional linear heat equation. Since the Darboux transformations DT⁡[xn]\mathrm{DT}[x^{n}] maps the equation of the form (42) with μ=n⁡(n−1)\mu=n(n-1) to the equation of the same form with μ=n⁡(n+1)\mu=n(n+1). As a result, beginning from n=1n=1 we derive the representation

u=(∂x−nx)(∂x−n−1x)⋯(∂x−1x)ϑ0(t,x)=DT[P1,P3,…,P2​n−1]ϑ0(t,x)\displaystyle u=\bigg(\partial_{x}-\frac{n}{x}\bigg)\bigg(\partial_{x}-\frac{n-1}{x}\bigg)\cdots\bigg(\partial_{x}-\frac{1}{x}\bigg)\vartheta^{0}(t,x)\ =\mathrm{DT}[P_{1},P_{3},\dots,P_{2n-1}]\vartheta^{0}(t,x) (43)

for an arbitrary solution of the equation of the form (42) with μ=n⁡(n+1)\mu=n(n+1), where ϑ0\vartheta^{0} is an arbitrary solution of the (1+1)-dimensional linear heat equation, for which μ=0\mu=0. Here PkP_{k} is the canonical heat polynomial of degree k∈ℕ∪{0}k\in\mathbb{N}\cup\{0\}, which is, for odd k=2​m−1k=2m-1 with m∈ℕm\in\mathbb{N}, of the form

P2​m−1​(t,x)=x2​m−1(2​m−1)!+t1!​x2​m−3(2​m−3)!+t22!​x2​m−5(2​m−5)!+⋯+tm−2(m−2)!​x33!+tm−1(m−1)!​x1!.\displaystyle P_{2m-1}(t,x)=\frac{x^{2m-1}}{(2m-1)!}+\frac{t}{1!}\frac{x^{2m-3}}{(2m-3)!}+\frac{t^{2}}{2!}\frac{x^{2m-5}}{(2m-5)!}+\cdots+\frac{t^{m-2}}{(m-2)!}\frac{x^{3}}{3!}+\frac{t^{m-1}}{(m-1)!}\frac{x}{1!}.

To check the second equality in (43), it suffices to prove that
